<meta>This page follows the title page of the first volume of the "Bibliotheque des Philosophes Chymiques" (1672). It lists the specific foundational alchemical texts included in this volume, ranging from legendary ancient sources like Hermes Trismegistus to then-contemporary 17th-century authors like Philalethes.</meta>

# VII. TREATISES CONTAINED
## in this first Volume of the Library
## of [Chemical] Philosophers.

I. *The Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus, with the Commentaries of Hortulanus.* <note>The Emerald Tablet is one of the most famous foundational texts of Hermeticism; "Hortulanus" is a Latinized name for an author often identified as Joannes de Garlandia.</note>

II. *The Turba Philosophorum <note>original: "La Tourbe des Philosophes"; the title is Latin for "The Assembly of the Philosophers"</note>, or the Assembly of the Disciples of Pythagoras, called the Code of all truth.*

III. *The Book of Nicolas Flamel, containing the explanation of the Hieroglyphic Figures which he had placed at the Cemetery of the Holy Innocents in Paris, with these same Figures, & those of Abraham the Jew, in Copperplate engraving.* <note>Nicolas Flamel (c. 1330–1418) was a French scribe who posthumously became the most famous legendary figure in French alchemy.</note>

IV. *The Book of the Natural Philosophy of Metals by Lord Bernard, Count of the Trevisan March, called the Trevisan.* <note>Bernard of Trevisan (1406–1490) was an influential Italian alchemist known for his travels in search of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>

V. *The Opuscule of D. Zachary, Gentleman of Guyenne.* <note>Denis Zacaire (1510–1556) was a French alchemist; his "Opuscule" or "Small Work" is a classic of the genre.</note>

VI. *Treatise on the Terrestrial Heaven by Wenceslaus Lavinius of Moravia.*

VII. *Philalethes, or the Open Entrance to the Closed Palace of the King.* <note>Philalethes (Greek for "Lover of Truth") was the pseudonym for a famous 17th-century alchemist, now widely identified as George Starkey.</note>

These last two Treatises have been newly translated, & the others revised & corrected against several Copies.

# PREFACE.

## FIRST PART.

### *On the Truth of the Science.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'L' featuring floral patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>

The intent I have to give to the Public in our own language a Collection of the chosen Works of the Philosophers, or of the most approved Authors, who from Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the founder of the "Hermetic" or alchemical tradition.</note> until now have written of the Transmutation <term>Transmutation: The Alchemical process of changing one substance, particularly a "base" metal, into another.</term> of imperfect Metals into Silver & into Gold: or (to speak more properly) of their Perfection, by means of the Powder of Projection <note>A form of the Philosopher's Stone, usually described as a heavy powder, intended to be "projected" or cast upon molten base metal to transform it.</note> which is otherwise called the Philosopher’s Stone; obliges me before all things to establish the truth of the Science, or of the Art, which teaches how to perform this Transmutation, & to show its possibility.

For if it is but a pure caprice of the imagination of men, as most are persuaded, & even those who appear the most sensible & who are otherwise very skilled in the other Sciences. If it is only a deception invented by Impostors, to abuse by the hope of an immense wealth the greedy & the simple; as one sees every day only too many examples. If it is at least only the work of the ambition of the human Spirit, which wants to rise with empire above the power of Nature; which flatters itself

They all confess that it is in their Books that they have learned to know the true ma-tter, and the only way to prepare it; in which consists the whole secret and the whole artifice. And they say that it is by their Writings alone that they have been instructed in the Operations and the Regimen <term>Regimen: The "Regimen of Fires," referring to the specific sequence and intensity of heat required during different stages of the alchemical process.</term> which are necessary to succeed therein.

But because, as has already been said, these Books—which, by the extraordinary Science they teach, ought to be so esteemed and sought after, if it be true—would on the contrary be very pernicious and very prejudicial if this same science were false and imaginary. To give belief to the authority of the Philoso-phers and credit to their Books; it is neces-sarily required to show that the Transmutation and the Philosopher’s Stone which they teach are true and possible.

To do this with some order, because one must first agree upon what one wishes to establish: I shall begin with the defi-nition of the Art of Chemistry <term>Chymie: In the 17th century, "Chymistry" encompassed both what we now call chemistry and the spiritual/metallic pursuits of alchemy.</term> which teaches how to perform Transmutation: then I shall give an idea of its Effect by the exact description I shall make of the Philosopher’s Stone; which is the thing in question. And thereafter, I shall prove its possi-bility by the two means through which one is accustomed to prove a contested truth, which are Au-thority and Reason. And because we are dealing here with a question of fact, I shall add Expe-rience <note>original: "Experience". Here referring to empirical demonstration or laboratory practice.</note>, which would suffice on its own to establish this truth, being in these kinds of matters the most assured and most convincing proof. And although I am undoubtedly the least enlightened...

...proof based on authority, on reason, and on experience. Let us begin with the first.

Although truth is not sufficiently or solidly supported nor strengthened by the testimony of men, unless it is supported by the revelation of God—who alone is infallible—it is nevertheless very certain that if one did not receive this proof, which is authorized by Divine and Human Laws, there would be nothing that could not be doubted. For if with Doctrine and Science, Probity of manners and Holiness of life are joined, it is undoubtedly true that their authority is all the more acceptable, as it is not believable that men so learned and so pious would have wanted to lie in the face of the whole earth, and pass down to all posterity an imposture of such consequence as an indubitable truth.

From air [comes] water, if the heat is overcome by the cold? For the one [air] was moist and hot; the other [water] cold and moist; so when the heat changes, it will be water. <note>original Greek: Ἐξ ἀέρος [ἢ] ὕδωρ, ἐὰν κρατηθῇ τὸ θερμὸν ὑπὸ τοῦ ψυχροῦ ; τὸ μὲν γὰρ ἦν ὑγρὸν καὶ θερμόν ; τὸ δὲ ψυχρὸν καὶ ὑγρόν · ὥστε μεταβάλλοντος τοῦ θερμοῦ ὕδωρ ἔσται.</note> Aristotle, book 2 of *On Generation and Corruption*, chapter 4.
</margin>
This reasoning is established, acknowledged in the second book of *On **Generation** and **Corruption***, that the **Elements** can change into one another. Here is how he speaks of it: *From **Air**, **Water** will be made, if the **heat** [of the Air] is overcome by the **Cold** [of the Water], because Air is hot and moist, and Water is cold and moist. And thus, once the heat is changed, it will be Water.* And all the **Scholastics** <note>Followers of the "School," the medieval university system that merged Aristotelian philosophy with Christian theology.</note> are of this same sentiment.

But there is cause for wonder that while remaining in agreement with their Master regarding the **Transmutation** of the Elements, they dare to assert that **Species** (that is to say, individuals of two different species) cannot change into one another. For in this, besides the fact that they are contrary to **Aristotle**, they manifestly deny **Experience**—and an Experience that occurs every day within themselves. Here it is: it is certain that **Wheat** and **Water** are not of the same species as **Blood**, **Flesh**, **Bones**, or the other **similar parts** <note>In ancient anatomy, "similar" or "homoeomerous" parts are tissues that are uniform throughout, like bone or fat, as opposed to complex organs like the heart.</note> of our bodies, which appear simple. Nevertheless, they cannot deny that once wheat is reduced to flour, and this flour is kneaded with water, **Bread** is made from it. That by eating this Bread and drinking Water, this Bread and this Water change into **Chyle** <term>Chyle: A milky fluid produced in the stomach and intestines during digestion, which ancient and medieval physicians believed was the "first stage" of blood production.</term> in the **Stomach**, and that this Chyle is a different species from the Bread and the Water we have taken. This Chyle then changes into another species different from itself, because it becomes **Blood** in the **Heart**; and this Blood, being carried throughout the body by the **Arteries**, changes into **Flesh** and **Bone**, and into all our other similar parts, which are all of different species.

Everyone knows that **Frogs** have at the beginning of their formation nothing less than the appearance & the shape of Frogs, being composed only of a large head and a small tail, & that they remain for a long time in this state before being entirely formed. The same thing happens to **Toads** which are made from seed, & by the ordinary way of Nature. And even if <insert>a</insert> **Aristotle** had not said that **Caterpillars** change into **Butterflies**, & that among these Caterpillars there are those that form on the green leaves of herbs, & especially on **cabbage**, no one could doubt it. But what will be said of the **Scoters** <note>original: "Macreuses," a type of sea duck. How should we name the production of **Rats**, **Spiders**, **Flies**, **Worms**, & an infinity of other **Insects**, of which the same Aristotle speaks <insert>b</insert> in the 5th Book of the *History of Animals*, which are born from the **putrefaction** of several things that have no resemblance—neither in their matter (at least in what the **School** <note>The Scholastic philosophers of the medieval universities.</note> calls *second matter* <term>Second Matter: In Aristotelian philosophy, this is matter that already possesses a specific form or identity (like wood or meat), as opposed to "Prime Matter" which is pure potential.</term>) nor in what it calls *qualities* <term>Qualities: The four primary characteristics (Hot, Cold, Moist, Dry) that define the state of matter.</term>—to these Insects & these other Animals that are formed from them?

For if experience shows us that the species of **Plants** & **Animals**, which are bodies made of parts of a different nature and which are more complex than **Metals**, change into one another every day? Why would one want to deny that the imperfect **Metals**—which are simpler Mixtures <note>In alchemical philosophy, a "mixture" or "mixt" refers to a compound formed from the primary elements.</note>, even though each of them is of a particular species—can be changed into **Silver** & **Gold**? And thus one can say that the matter is all ready and quite disposed to receive **Transmutation** <term>Transmutation: The alchemical transformation of one element or metal into another, specifically base metals into noble ones.</term>.

But just as it is not enough to have the proper Materials all ready to build a Palace, if one does not have the Architect to direct the design, & the Workers to build it. It is not enough that the imperfect Metals be capable of receiving Transmutation; that nothing can prevent them from being converted into Silver & Gold, and that their Mercury has every disposition to receive this final perfection. It must also be shown that the **Powder of projection** <term>Powder of Projection: A highly concentrated form of the Philosopher’s Stone, which was "projected" or cast onto molten base metals to transmute them.</term>, which is the Agent that can produce this marvelous effect by giving **fixity** & **Tincture** <note>"Fixity" is the quality of a substance that allows it to endure fire without being consumed; "Tincture" is the transformative color and quality the Stone imparts to the metal.</note> to this Mercury of the imperfect Metals, is possible, and that it can be made.

I admit that it is quite difficult to prove this possibility demonstratively; both because the **Philosophers** <note>In this context, "Philosophers" specifically refers to alchemists, often called "Philosophers by Fire."</note>—who are very reserved on this matter and who with good reason make a great mystery of their **Science**—carefully hide the Causes and Principles of this marvelous production of **Art** and **Nature**; or if they do speak of them, it is only in metaphorical and very obscure terms, which most often have two contrary meanings; and also because the question here being to know if a thing can be done, only **experience** itself is the true proof, and the only thing that can fully convince one of this possibility, because only **Experience** <note>The author uses "Experience" to mean what we would now call "experimental evidence."</note> can allow its effect to be seen.

If nevertheless, in establishing this possibility upon the proof that the **School** <note>Refers to Scholasticism, the traditional philosophical and theological system taught in medieval and early modern universities.</note> calls Negative, one could remain satisfied, it would not be difficult to show that there is no impossibility in making the **Powder of Projection** <term>Powder of Projection: A highly concentrated form of the Philosopher's Stone, which, when "projected" or cast upon molten base metals, was said to transmute them into gold or silver.</term>. First, there is no convincing reason that can demonstrate it to be impossible. Secondly, this impossibility could only come from the weakness of either the **Matter**, or that of the **Agent**. It cannot come from the matter, since it is the same that **Nature** uses to produce **Gold**, and since it is **Gold** itself, to which through preparation and through **cooking** <note>original: "cuisson"—the prolonged heating of alchemical substances in a furnace to reach a state of perfection.</note>, one gives a fixity and a **tincture** <note>In alchemy, a "tincture" is a potent essence or soul of a metal that has the power to "stain" and transform the properties of other substances.</note> more abundant and greater than those it had received in the **Mines**.

The impossibility cannot come from the **Agent** either, which is twofold; one acting from without, and the other from within: **Art** and **Nature**. The first does nothing other than prepare the **Matter**, and maintain the heat from without at a degree necessary to perform the cooking:

...grains of its own nature, and that each of these grains, when likewise placed in the earth, produces several other similar grains in the same way? And this **Multiplication** <note>In alchemy, "Multiplication" is the process by which the power and quantity of the Philosopher's Stone are increased, often compared to the way a single seed produces a whole ear of corn.</note> occurs unceasingly, and to a greater or lesser degree, according to whether the earth is better or worse prepared. It is true that this Grain destroys itself in order to produce several others; but it is also true that this is less a destruction that happens to it than a **Multiplication** and a regeneration that takes place, since all the grains it produces are but a diffusion and an outpouring, so to speak, of this single grain, which has shared and divided itself into several grains by means of the nourishment provided by the earth, from which this same grain had drawn its sustenance and growth. The same is true for the multiplication of the **Philosopher's Stone** <term>Pierre Philosophale: The legendary substance sought by alchemists, capable of transmuting base metals into gold and acting as a universal medicine.</term>. A grain of this Stone is like a seed which, being placed in the **Philosophers' Mercury** <term>Mercure des Philosophes: This is not common quicksilver, but a "living" or "philosophical" mercury that alchemists believed was the true "soil" or "womb" required for the Stone to grow.</term>, which is its own earth from which this grain and seed were formed, fructifies in this earth and produces several other similar grains. In this manner, each multiplication is like a new sowing (to use the laborers' term) which always produces a new and most abundant harvest, because the earth where this seed germinates is of the same nature as the seed itself that it receives. Just as wheat grows more abundantly in land that is well-manured, because the manure comes from a vegetable nature just as the wheat does; being nothing other than the rotted straw and stubble of wheat, and the hay and herbs that the animal has digested.

For of all these different names that they give to their Mercury, it is found that each of these names explains either a principle, or a property, or an operation, or a particular circumstance. And thus there is no contradiction, neither between these names nor between the **Philosophers** <note>The author uses "Philosophers" to mean "Adepts" or true alchemists who have mastered the art.</note>, who are found to be in conformity in all things and everywhere.

This goes so far that even without having had any communication together, without having seen nor known each other, without having read one another's **Works**, they have explained and clarified one another, and one has added what the others had omitted; and very often, a single one has said clearly what all the others had shrouded and said very obscurely. This is evident testimony that although they have explained themselves differently, they have nonetheless all known and intended to say only the same thing. And in effect, if the **Philosopher's Stone** was only something contrived by one among them, if it were only an imposture that the Philosophers had taken from one another: if it were only a Fable that they had borrowed and copied from the Books of those who had invented it: without doubt they would have used the same words... <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "paroles."</note>

This signifies that Mercury, through the care of the Artist <note>In alchemical texts, "the Artist" refers to the chemist or alchemist performing the work.</note>, goes from being volatile to being **fixed** <term>Fixed: In alchemy, "fixing" a substance means turning a volatile or evaporating gas/liquid into a stable solid that can withstand fire.</term> and becomes an admirable Medicine. It is by this means that Medea (whose name means "Medicine") made Aeson young again, because one of the effects of the Stone is to preserve health and prolong life.

The Fable of the Gardens of the Hesperides, where there were trees that bore Golden fruits, guarded by a dragon who was always watchful, and whom Hercules was obliged to kill in order to pick these fruits, still cannot be well understood nor explained otherwise than as the Philosopher's Stone. For the watchful Dragon is nothing other than Mercury, which is in perpetual and volatile movement, until Hercules—who represents the industrious Artist—has killed this Monster; that is to say, has fixed it with much difficulty. Then he has in his possession the Golden Tree of which the **Cosmopolite** <note>The "Cosmopolite" was the pseudonym of Michael Sendivogius (1566–1636), a famous Polish alchemist and chemist.</note> speaks, which bears Golden fruits and which multiplies without any need for replanting.

One could relate here, as evidence of the Philosopher's Stone, what Suidas says under the word **Chemistry** <note>original Greek: "χημία" (chemia).</note>: that Diocletian, having defeated the Egyptians who had revolted, treated them very poorly. He ordered a search for all the books of the Ancients that treated of Chemistry—which is the art of making Gold and Silver—and had them burned. This was done so that by depriving them of the means to enrich themselves, they would no longer have the boldness to revolt based on the confidence of their riches.

It is therefore necessary to show that Flamel—whom one cannot deny created these Hieroglyphic Figures (since his name and his image are present there)—is indeed the Author of the Book that explains them so well. Here are the proofs.

Nicolas Flamel was born in Paris, but one cannot say for certain either the year of his birth or the time of his death, because there are no Baptismal or Death Registers so ancient at St. Jacques de la Boucherie <note>Saint-Jacques-de-la-Boucherie was Flamel’s parish church. While most of the church was destroyed during the French Revolution, its famous Gothic tower, the Tour Saint-Jacques, still stands in central Paris.</note>, which was his parish and the place of his burial. Nevertheless, by the date of his Testament <note>A will or legal declaration of a person's wishes regarding their property after death.</note>, which is from Sunday, November 22, 1416; and by a Contract signed by the Executors of the Will of Perrenelle his wife, on Tuesday, the 2nd day of April, before Easter, in the year 1419, where these words appear: *the late Perrenelle, wife of the late Nicolas Flamel* <note>original: "feüe Perrenelle femme de feu Nicolas Flamel." The term "feu/feüe" was a standard legal term for the recently deceased.</note>; there is a strong appearance that he died toward the end of that year, that is to say, in the month of March of the year 1419. It is likely that this Act was made a few days after Flamel’s death, because he was one of the Testamentary Executors of his wife. And since the Foreword of his Book is dated the year 1419—which he surely wrote only a short time before his death, although he had completed the Book itself as early as 1413. Thus, by tracing back through the course of his life, one can conjecture that he must have been born in the time of Philip of Valois <note>Philip VI (reigned 1328–1350), the first king of the House of Valois.</note>, who began to reign at the end of the year 1328, or at the very most under the reign of Charles the Fair <note>Charles IV (reigned 1322–1328), the last king of the direct Capetian line.</note> who succeeded Philip the Tall in the year 1322. It is not believable that Flamel lived, according to the ordinary course of Nature, much more than 91 or 97 years. His parents were poor, apparently leaving him no wealth other than the house where he lived and where he died. This house, which he gave to the Church, is in the street of the Scribes <note>Rue des Écrivains. He practiced no other profession throughout his life. For in his Last Will and Testament, he takes no other title than that of "Writer."

As Flamel earned his living by copying books and by writing inventories and accounts, he found by chance during some inventory the *Book of Abraham the Jew*, which he purchased. It appears, as he tells it, that this book had been stolen from the Jews or found hidden in one of their houses when they were pillaged and driven out of this Kingdom under Philip the Tall <note>Philip V of France, who reigned from 1316 to 1322.</note>, who banished them and confiscated all their property in the year 1319, 1320, or 1321. He had no sooner read it than, having recognized that it taught how to make the <term>Philosopher’s Stone</term> <note>The legendary alchemical substance capable of turning base metals into gold and providing the "elixir of life."</note>, he became so passionate about it that he always had it in his hands; he read it or dreamed incessantly of this Science which was clearly explained therein, with the exception of the "First Agent"—that is to say, the <term>Mercury of the Philosophers</term> <note>In alchemy, this is not common mercury, but a theoretical "prime matter" or secret ingredient required to begin the transformation of metals.</note>—which was represented there only under <term>hieroglyphical figures</term> <note>Symbolic, pictorial illustrations used to hide alchemical secrets from the uninitiated.</note>. Flamel, having such a great treasure in his possession, thought only of using it as a true philosopher and a good Christian should; that is to say, for the glory of God and for the relief of the poor, whom he assisted in such a way that his left hand did not know what his right hand was doing <note>A biblical reference to Matthew 6:3, signifying that his charity was performed secretly and without pride.</note>. This is not counting what he did in Boulogne-sur-Mer.

Because Flamel performed his charities without noise or fanfare—both because charities done in this manner are much more pleasing to God, and because he did not wish to be discovered—we have known and convincing evidence of everything he did in this city in only four places, where the marks of his work are evident and undeniable.

In the 20th article, he gives his relatives the sum of only forty <term>livres</term> <note>The standard currency of account in France at the time.</note>, which clearly shows that he had no ancestral property; for by Article 291 of the *Custom of Paris* <note>The traditional civil law of the Paris region until the Napoleonic Code.</note>, under the title of Wills, no person may dispose by testament of their own inherited property except *for a fifth only and no more, even if it were for a charitable cause.* <note>original: "du quint seulement & non plus avant, encore que ce fust pour chose pitoyable."</note> And thus the other four-fifths must belong to the heirs of the family line. He survived his will and did not die until three years later.

<meta>This page continues the author’s systematic rebuttal of Scholastic objections to alchemy. Having previously addressed the argument that "artificial" heat is an "accident" that cannot produce a "substance," the author now explores the logic of the "First Cause" (God) and "Second Causes" (nature) to prove that alchemical gold-making is consistent with both theology and natural law.</meta>

-># PREFACE.<-

Secondly, since it is the heat of the Sun that produces gold in the bowels of the earth, there is no more inconvenience or impossibility in the heat of fire—which is of the same nature—producing the same effect. But this heat, they say, only serves to prepare the matter of gold. Let them show me then, if they please, who is the **Principal Agent** that brings about this production. Is it the Gold that is already formed? There is more likelihood that it is this than any other cause, since every thing produces its like. But the same difficulty is met with regarding this first Gold. And if it is Gold that has this effect, then Gold has the power to multiply itself. Besides, it is Gold which the <term>Philosophers</term><note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers to alchemists or natural philosophers who study the secrets of nature.</note> use for their works. Thus, the Chemists can rest easy on that account.

Will it be the <term>First Cause</term><note>In medieval and early modern philosophy, the "First Cause" refers to God, the ultimate source of all action in the universe.</note>? Undoubtedly. For it never fails those of the <term>School</term><note>The "School" refers to Scholasticism, the dominant philosophical and theological system in European universities during the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> in their time of need. And they assert that, at the critical moment, it always makes up for the failure of <term>Second Causes</term><note>Natural agents or physical forces that act as intermediaries for the First Cause (God).</note>. But the <term>Matter of the Philosophers</term><note>The starting material or "prima materia" used in alchemical operations.</note> is the same as that which Nature uses. It has the same dispositions (since they insist on "dispositions") through the same heat. Why then would the First Cause not act here if there is no other cause to do so, since they insist that it acts unfailingly and necessarily when all things are ready and prepared, and there is no other Cause to act? Once again, we are vindicated. Thus, in whatever sense one turns the matter—whether one wishes for heat to perform the <term>Work</term><note>The *Magnum Opus* or Great Work: the process of creating the Philosopher’s Stone.</note> of the Philosophers, or for gold to bring about the production, or whether one must have recourse to the First Cause—this Work cannot fail.

### The Book of Nicolas Flamel.

The III. Treatise is the Book of *Nicolas Flamel*, a Parisian, which contains the explanation of the Hieroglyphic Figures <note>The "Hieroglyphic Figures" refers to a famous series of allegorical alchemical paintings.</note> that he had placed at the Cemetery of the Holy Innocents <note>original: "Cimetiere des SS. This Book is certainly by Flamel, as I have demonstrated. He wrote it in Latin, which I have been unable to find despite all the research I have conducted; had I found it, I would have produced a new Translation. Things heard through the ear stir the mind more slowly than those which are placed before the faithful eyes. Horace, *Art of Poetry*, line 180. <note>original Latin: "Segniùs irritant animos demissa per aurem, Quam quæ sunt oculis subjecta fidelibus."</note>

## THE TREVISAN.

The fourth treatise of this volume is the Book of the **Trevisan**, who, because of his sincerity and his simplicity, is called **the good Trevisan**; he was a person of quality <note>Meaning a person of noble rank or high social standing.</note> from Germany, who nevertheless wrote in French. For Dorneus, a German, translated it into Latin from the French original, just as he also translated Zachaire, and the Treatises in French rhymes which are printed following it.

Basil <note>Likely Basil Valentine, a legendary alchemical figure; his "Colloquy of the Spirit and Albert" refers to a dialogue between a spirit and Albertus Magnus.</note> says of the Trevisan <note>Bernard of Treviso (1406–1490), a famous Italian alchemist who spent his life and fortune seeking the Philosopher’s Stone.</note> that he spoke the truth twice and a falsehood once in the *Colloquy of the Spirit and Albert*. He was mistaken, however, when he states in the first part of his book that the Bible says it was *Hermes* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy.</note> who entered the *Valley of Hebron* after the Deluge and found *seven tables* upon which the *seven Liberal Arts* were engraved. For there is no such account in the Bible. However, in the history of the Jews by Josephus—the *Antiquities of the Jews* <note>original: "Antiquitez Iudaïques"</note>, Book 1, Chapter 2—it is said that the *Children of Seth*, knowing that the world was destined to perish by water and by fire, erected two columns, one of stone and the other of brick. Upon these they engraved the knowledge of astrology which they had learned from their father, for fear that this science might be lost before mankind could be instructed in it. And Josephus adds that the stone column was still visible in Syria in his own time.

He wrote with fine organization and summarized the books of the Philosophers <note>In alchemical texts, "the Philosophers" refers to the long lineage of alchemical authorities like Hermes, Geber, or Lull.</note>. The author of the *Chemical Library* <note>original: "Bibliotheque Chymique"; likely referring to a compendium of alchemical texts such as those by Jean Manget or William Salmon.</note> observes in his preface that there is an error in the timeline Zachaire recounts from the start of the Work until the end. Doubtless, he means that Zachaire allows too little time for the preparation and for the "Great Work," which he seems to claim he completed entirely in almost a year. For he states that he arrived home at the beginning of Lent <note>original: "Caresme"; the forty-day period of fasting before Easter, often used as a chronological marker.</note>, that he began to work on Easter Day <note>original: "Pasques"</note>, and that he performed the projection <note>The "projection" is the final stage of alchemy where the Philosopher's Stone is cast onto molten base metal to transmute it into gold.</note> on Easter Day, which was the first day of the following year. But certainly Zachaire had the Mercury of the Philosophers <note>term: Mercury of the Philosophers (The secret "First Matter" of alchemy, not to be confused with common quicksilver).</note> already prepared when he arrived home. And the work he performed during Lent, after his arrival, was simply to arrange what was necessary to put his Matter <note>The physical substance being transformed in the alchemical vessel.</note> into the "cooking" <note>original: "cuisson"; the process of applying steady heat to the matter, also known as "coction."</note>.

---

### *The Terrestrial Heaven of Levinus.*

**THE SIXTH** Treatise is the *Terrestrial Heaven* of Wenceslaus Levinus of Moravia, which is a province near Hungary, under the jurisdiction of the Kingdom of Bohemia. I cannot say at what time he wrote. This Treatise is very short, but it is excellent. The end of this Treatise has been translated into French verse, where he speaks of the Mercury of the Philosophers; of which he says very specific things, but in the manner of the Philosophers—by way of riddles and obscurity. I have translated it into French, and I have had placed in italics several words that I added to make the meaning more intelligible and complete.

<margin>It is difficult for one following foreign languages not to stumble somewhere. St. Jerome in the preface to the *Chronicle* of Eusebius. <note>original: "Difficile est alienas linguas insequētem non alicubi excidere. D. Hieronymus in præf. Chronic. Euseb."</note></margin>
What he says of Elijah is taken from Paracelsus, who says in one of his books that after him will come Elijah the Artist, who will teach what is currently hidden <note>Elijah the Artist (A messianic figure in alchemical lore, predicted by Paracelsus to arrive in the future and reveal all the secrets of nature and the Great Work to the world).</note>. I have nothing more to say about the translation I have made of it, following the remarks I have added after that translation. I do not doubt that I may have been mistaken, because, as a Father of the Church says, it is difficult, when translating *that which is written in a foreign language*, not to make some fault. But I have tried to capture the author’s meaning as much as I have been able to discern it. It is said that this same author wrote a dialogue on the *Alkahest* <term>Alkahest (The theoretical universal solvent of the alchemists, said to be capable of reducing any body to its first matter)</term>, which I have not seen. However, he has sufficiently obliged the public with this work alone. Thus, *let us be content with this Cato* <note>original: "contenti simus hoc Catone"; a Latin idiom meaning one should be satisfied with the authoritative material already provided, referencing the stern Roman statesman Cato.</note>.

I have added at the end a list of Terms of the Art and of old French words found in Trevisan and Zachaire <note>Bernard Trevisan (1406–1490) and Denis Zachaire (1510–1556) were famous alchemists; their works often used archaic or obscure French terminology.</note>, which I have explained, having preferred to place them at the end of the book rather than in the margin; for in this way they will not clutter the text, and will only be for those who do not understand the Latin language, from which the greater part is derived. I have had them set in italic type to distinguish them from the Terms of the Art which are in small capitals, and which I have explained very briefly; reserving a more extensive explanation for the *Dictionary*, which will be the last volume of our Library. If there are some mysterious terms for which I have not given an explanation, it is because I have not understood them myself. For after all, *I am Davus, not Oedipus* <note>original: "Davus sum, non Oedipus"; a common Latin expression meaning "I am a simple man, not a solver of riddles," contrasting the servant Davus from Roman comedy with the riddle-solving Oedipus of Greek myth.</note>. I mean to say that I do not have the gift of divination to uncover what the Philosophers have so carefully and intentionally hidden, because they are too protective of their Secret.

as much as I was able; and despite the care I have taken to vary this *Discourse* to make it less unpleasant, I do not doubt that it will seem far too long, and that it will be *very tedious*. I even know that it will be useless to those who are already advanced. Therefore, it is not for them that I have made it, but only for those who are beginning, and who wish to seriously apply themselves to this Science and to the search for the Philosopher's Stone. It is to those people that I can say this Discourse, which is founded upon the Authority of the Philosophers, should not be useless nor unpleasant: because by confirming them in this truth, and providing them in advance with a true idea of the Great Work <term>Great Work (The *Magnum Opus*, the entire process of creating the Philosopher's Stone)</term>, they will make more progress in their reading, they will be more assured in the views they hold, and they will not stray so easily from the only path one must follow to reach this knowledge. And so that they may read the Books of the Philosophers even more usefully, and distance themselves from all errors and sophistications, I shall finish this Preface with several maxims that I have drawn from our Authors; these will serve as a guide for Apprentices, and for myself, in our Study, and in the project that we may form of their Great Work through the reading of the Philosophers.

### I. MAXIM.

There is nothing real and true in Philosophy <note>In this context, "Philosophy" refers specifically to Hermetic Philosophy or Alchemy, the "search for wisdom" through the study of nature's secrets.</note> except for the Philosopher's Stone alone. *I knew well*, says Trevisan <note>Bernard Trevisan (1406–1490), an Italian nobleman and celebrated alchemist whose works were highly influential in the 17th century.</note>, *that anything other than the Stone was false*. And elsewhere, *There is no other Tincture but ours*. Thus, all that are called *Particulars* <term>Particulars (Minor or localized alchemical processes that aim to transmute small amounts of metal or improve specific qualities, which many "true" alchemists considered fraudulent or incomplete distractions)</term>. All the *Graduations*, *Augmentations*, and *Tincture of the Moon* <note>The "Tincture of the Moon" refers to the specific transmutation of base metals into silver, as opposed to the "Tincture of the Sun" for gold.</note> which are made other than by the true Powder of Projection <term>Powder of Projection (The final, potent form of the Philosopher's Stone, which is "projected" or cast upon molten base metals to transmute them into gold or silver)</term> are false.

MAXIM.** One must not undertake to work, says Zachaire <note>Denis Zachaire (1510–1556), a French alchemist famous for his autobiographical account of his long and expensive search for the Stone.</note>, until one truly knows the thing, and until one sees the possibility of it, and all the operations and the sequences of the Work until its final perfection; as if one had it present before one's eyes. And that one understands the Work through the Philosophers, and the Philosophers through the Work, so that one can reconcile them all, and that one finds no more contradictions in their Writings. It is not that there are many things in the books of the Philosophers, says Nathanael Albineus <note>Nathaniel Albineus was the physician and editor who compiled the *Bibliotheca Chemica Contracta* (The Contracted Chemical Library) in 1653.</note> who is the Author of the *Chemical Library*, that the Philosophers themselves would not know how to understand, because they make allusion to certain things, and to certain circumstances, that it is not easy to guess: but these are not essential things.

**III. MAXIM.** Whoever knows the Science will never say so, except to a faithful friend. Because the Philosophers are so jealous of their Science, that they would hide it from themselves if it were possible for them. And thus all those who say they know the Philosopher's Stone, and who ask for money to make it, evidently show by that, that they do not know it: because they would prefer never to make it than to tell it for money. Secrecy being the essential mark of a Philosopher. Which certainly comes from the too great ease and simplicity of the thing <note>Alchemists often claimed the process was actually very simple once understood, which is why it had to be hidden; otherwise, the whole world would do it and destabilize the economy.</note>.

# PREFACE.

IV. MAXIM. There is only one single metallic matter, and only one way to perform the Great Work <term>Great Work (The *Magnum Opus*; the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone)</term>, which is natural, simple, and easy, far from being encumbered by so many fantastic operations that the Sophists <term>Sophists (In an alchemical context, "sophists" were fraudulent or misguided practitioners who used overly complex or unnatural methods)</term> imagine. And this is so because the Philosophers assert it, and because otherwise they would never have been able to discover it. The entire difficulty lies only in making the Mercury of the Philosophers <term>Mercury of the Philosophers (The essential "first matter" or specialized solvent required to begin the work, not to be confused with common quicksilver)</term>.

V. MAXIM. The Philosopher's Stone is not found by chance, says *Philalethes* <note>Eirenaeus Philalethes was the pseudonym of a famous 17th-century alchemist, often identified as George Starkey, whose name means "peaceful lover of truth."</note>. Because it is a certain and true Science, and one which is founded upon the infallible principles of Nature. And it is true and possible only because it is natural. Thus, those who work without knowing what they must do, and without knowing the thing itself, will never find anything.

VI. MAXIM. One needs to incur almost no expense to make the Philosopher's Stone, says *Philalethes*. And undoubtedly the costs do not exceed twenty or thirty pistoles <term>Pistole (A gold coin of the era, used here to indicate a modest sum compared to the fortunes many lost in failed alchemical pursuits)</term> in total. Thus, those who wish to engage us in great expenses to perform the Work are ignorant men and impostors, who must not be believed; the most certain path being to keep the money one has, and not to make any foolish expenditure for it; remembering the Spanish Proverb, which says *Proven alchemy is to have an income and spend nothing* <note>original: "Alquimia probada tener renta y no gastar nada." This is a play on words suggesting that the most successful "alchemy" is simply financial frugality.</note>. That it is a sure Philosopher's Stone to have a good income, and spend nothing, or at least to manage it well.

VII. THE LAST MAXIM. And which ought to have been the first, because it is the most significant of all. It is that without the blessing of God it is impossible that we could ever succeed in such a great design. That it is, as has been said, from this sole Father of Lights that we must hope for the knowledge and revelation of

# CHAPTER ONE.

## The Art of Alchemy is true and certain.

The Philosopher says: *It is true*, namely that the Art of Alchemy has been given to us. *Without lie*, he says this to convince those who say that the Science is lying, that is to say, false. *Certain*, that is to say experienced <note>In the language of the period, "experienced" refers to that which has been proven through "experiment" or practical work.</note>, for everything that is experienced is very certain. *And most true*, for the most true <term>Sun</term> <note>In alchemy, the "Sun" (Sol) typically refers to gold or the perfected state of matter achieved through the Great Work.</note> is procreated by the Art.

He says most true in the superlative, because the Sun engendered by this Art surpasses every natural Sun in all properties, both medicinal and others.

## CHAPTER II.

### *The Stone must be divided into two parts.*

Next, he touches upon the operation of the Stone, saying: *That which is below is as that which is above.* He says this because the Stone is divided into two principal parts by the <term>Magistery</term> <note>The "Magistery" refers to the entire technical process of the alchemical art and the mastery required to complete the Great Work.</note>; namely, into the superior part which ascends upward, and into the inferior part which remains below, fixed <note>In alchemy, "fixed" describes a substance that is stable and does not evaporate or change when exposed to heat.</note> and clear. And yet, these two parts agree in virtue. This is why he says: *And that which is above is as that which is below.* Certainly, this division is necessary. *To perform the miracles of one thing.* That is to say, of the Stone; for the inferior part is the Earth, which is the nurse and the ferment; and the superior part is the Soul, which gives life to the entire Stone and resurrects it. This is why, once the separation and conjunction are performed, many miracles come to pass in the secret work of nature.

## CHAPTER III.

### *The Stone has within itself the four Elements.*

AND *as all things have been and have come from one by the meditation of one.* Here he gives an example, saying: just as all things have been and have come forth from one—that is to say, from a confused globe or a confused mass <note>Original: "masse confuse." This refers to the "First Matter" or primal chaos from which God created the universe, and which the alchemist seeks to replicate in his flask.</note>—by the meditation—that is to say, by the thought and creation of one—that is to say, of God Almighty. *So all things were born*—that is to say, have come forth—*from this thing.*

## CHAPTER IV.

### *The Stone has a father and a mother, which are the Sun and the Moon.*

Just as we see that an animal naturally engenders several other animals similar to itself: so the Sun artificially engenders the Sun by the virtue of the multiplication of the Stone <note>Multiplication is the stage in the "Great Work" where the power and quantity of the Philosopher's Stone are increased.</note>. This is why it follows, *The Sun is its father*, that is to say, the gold of the Philosophers <note>The "Gold of the Philosophers" is not common bullion, but a refined, living philosophical principle representing the masculine, active, and "fixed" quality of the work.</note>. And because in all natural generations, there must be a place suitable for receiving the seeds, with some conformity of resemblance in part; so it is necessary that in this artificial generation of the Stone, the Sun has a matter which is like a matrix <note>The "matrix" refers to a womb or a specialized vessel where the alchemical "conception" takes place.</note> suitable for receiving its sperm and its tincture <note>A "tincture" is a potent alchemical liquid or soul-essence capable of transforming and coloring base metals into gold.</note>. And that is the silver of the Philosophers. This is why it follows, *and the Moon is its mother.*

This refers to the seventh line of the Emerald Tablet. In alchemical theory, the "wind" represents the volatile, spiritualized state of the matter (the Air) which carries the life-force or "soul" of the Stone.</note> It is well known that the wind is air, and air is life, and life is the soul, of which I have already spoken above, that it vivifies the entire Stone. ### CHAPTER VII.

#### *The cleansing of the Stone.*

Next, he teaches how the Stone must multiply; but beforehand, he sets forth the <term>cleansing</term> <note>Original: "mondification." A technical term for the purification or purging of dross from the matter.</note> of it and the separation of its parts, saying: *You shall separate the earth from the fire, the subtle from the thick, gently with great industry.* <note>Line 9 of the Emerald Tablet.</note> "Gently" means little by little, not by violence, but with spirit and skill, namely, by the <term>philosophical dung</term> or manure. <note>Original: "fient ou fumier philosophal." This refers to a method of providing a gentle, steady, and natural heat for "digesting" the matter, often achieved in early alchemy by burying vessels in a heap of fermenting horse manure.</note> *You shall separate*, that is to say, you shall dissolve; for dissolution is the separation of parts. *The earth from the fire, the subtle from the thick*, that is to say the dregs and the impurity from the fire, from the air, from the water, and from the entire substance of the Stone, so that it remains entirely without filth.

## CHAPTER VIII.

->The non-fixed part of the Stone must separate<-
->the fixed part and elevate it.<-

Once the Stone has been thus prepared, it can then be <term>multiplied</term> <note>Multiplication is the stage in the alchemical process where the power and quantity of the Philosopher's Stone are increased.</note>. He now introduces the multiplication, and speaks of its easy liquefaction or fusion through the virtue it possesses of entering and penetrating both hard and soft bodies, saying: *It ascends from the Earth to the Heaven, and descends again to the Earth.* <note>original: "Il monte de la Terre au Ciel, & derechef descend en Terre." This is a key precept of the Emerald Tablet describing the circulation of the matter.</note> It must be carefully noted here that although our Stone, in its first operation, is divided into four parts which constitute the four <term>Elements</term> <note>The classic building blocks: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note>; nevertheless (as has been stated above), there are two principal parts within it: one that ascends on high, which is called the <term>non-fixed</term> or the <term>volatile</term> <note>A substance that vaporizes or "takes flight" when heated.</note>; and the other which remains fixed below, which is called the <term>earth</term> or the <term>ferment</term>, as has been said. But one must have a large quantity of the non-fixed part and give it to the Stone when it is very pure and without dross; and it must be given so many times through the <term>Magistery</term> <note>The "Magistery" refers to the expert practice and completion of the alchemical Great Work.</note> that the entire Stone, by the power of the spirit, is carried upward, <term>subliming</term> <note>Sublimation: the process of turning a solid into vapor to purify it, here symbolizing the spiritualization of the material.</note> it and making it subtle. And this is what the Philosopher <note>Hermes Trismegistus.</note> says: *It ascends from the Earth to the Heaven.*

### CHAPTER XI.

#### *The Magistery imitates the creation of the Universe.*

**THE PHILOSOPHER** <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the purported author of the Emerald Tablet.</note> then gives an example of the composition of his stone, saying, *thus the world was created*; that is to say, our Stone is made in the same way that the world was created. For the first things of the whole world, and everything that has been in the world, was first a confused mass and a <term>chaos</term> <note>In alchemy, chaos refers to the "First Matter" (Materia Prima)—the raw, unrefined substance before it is acted upon by the alchemist.</note> without order, as was said above. And afterwards, by the artifice of the Sovereign Creator, this confused mass, having been admirably separated and rectified, was divided into four <term>Elements</term> <note>The four classical elements: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water, which alchemists believed were the building blocks of all matter.</note>: and because of this separation, various and different things are made. In this way also, various things can be made by the production and arrangement of our <term>Work</term> <note>Often called the "Great Work" (Magnum Opus), this is the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, and this by the separation of different Elements from different bodies. *From this shall come and proceed wonderful adaptations.* <note>original: "De cecy feront & sortiront d'admirables adaptations."</note> That is to say, if you separate the Elements, wonderful compositions suited to our Work will be made in the composition of our Stone, by the joining of the rectified Elements. *Of which*—that is to say, of which wonderful things proper to this—*the means, namely how to proceed, is here.*

<note>Magistery: The "Magistery" refers to the entire process of creating the Philosopher's Stone, or the Stone itself in its perfected state. Rectification: The process of purifying a substance through repeated distillation or refinement.</note>

<summary>This chapter draws a direct parallel between the divine creation of the universe from chaos and the alchemical creation of the Philosopher's Stone through the separation and refinement of elements. It establishes the "Great Work" as a microcosm of the cosmic process governed by the Sovereign Creator.</summary>

## CHAPTER XII.

### *Enigmatic declaration of the matter of the Stone.*

That is why I have been called Hermes Trismegistus <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the father of alchemy. His name means "Hermes the Thrice-Greatest."</note>, which is to say, Mercury thrice-great. After the Philosopher <note>Referring again to Hermes Trismegistus.</note> has taught the composition of the Stone, he shows here covertly what our Stone is made of, by naming himself: first, so that his disciples who attain this science will always remember his name. Nevertheless, he also touches upon what the Stone is made of, saying next: *Having the three parts of the Philosophy of the whole world* <note>original: "Ayant les trois parties de la Philosophie de tout le monde"</note>, because everything in the world, having matter and form, is composed of the four <term>Elements</term> <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note>. Now, although there are an infinite number of things in the world that compose it and make up its parts, the Philosopher nonetheless divides and reduces them all to three parts; namely, into the mineral, vegetable, and animal parts. He possessed the true knowledge of all of these—either together or separately—through the "operation of the Sun," which is the composition of the Stone. And it is for this reason that he says, *having the three parts of the Philosophy of the whole world*, all three of which are contained within the Stone alone; that is to say, in the <term>Mercury of the Philosophers</term> <note>In alchemy, this is not common quicksilver, but a purified, "living" essence or spirit extracted from matter, believed to be the essential ingredient of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>.

<note>original vocabulary: Table d'Emeraude (Emerald Tablet), Hermes Trismegiste (Hermes Trismegistus), Mercure (Mercury), Pierre Philosophale (Philosopher's Stone), quatre Elements (four Elements), minérale (mineral), végétale (vegetable), animale (animal), Soleil (Sun), Mercure des Philosophers (Mercury of the Philosophers)</note>

<summary>This chapter explains why the author is called Hermes Trismegistus and reveals that the "three parts of philosophy" (mineral, vegetable, and animal) are all unified within the Mercury of the Philosophers.</summary>

# CHAPTER XIII.

## *Why the Stone is called perfect.*

This Stone is called perfect because it contains within itself the nature of mineral, vegetable, and animal things. This is why it is called triple, or rather triune—that is to say, three-in-one—having four natures (namely the four <term>Elements</term> <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water, which alchemists believed were the building blocks of all matter.</note>) and three colors: black, white, and red <note>These colors correspond to the three main stages of the alchemical process: Nigredo (blackness/putrefaction), Albedo (whiteness/purification), and Rubedo (redness/perfection).</note>. It is also called the "grain of wheat," which, unless it dies, remains alone; but if it dies [as was said above, when it joins in the <term>conjunction</term> <note>The union of opposites, such as the "King" and "Queen" or Sulfur and Mercury, which results in the death of the initial forms and the birth of something new.</note>], it brings forth much fruit—that is to say, when the operations of which we have spoken are completed. O friend Reader! If you know the operation of the Stone, I have told you the truth; and if you do not know it, I have told you nothing. What I have said concerning the "operation of the Sun" is accomplished and finished. That is to say, what has been said regarding the operation of the Stone of three colors and four natures, which exist in a single thing—namely, in the <term>Philosophical Mercury</term> <note>The essential, spiritual "seed" or medium of the alchemical work, not to be confused with common quicksilver.</note> alone—is completed and finished.

---

## THE ASSEMBLY
# OF THE PHILOSOPHERS
### OR THE GATHERING OF THE DISCIPLES OF PYTHAGORAS, CALLED THE CODE OF TRUTH.

Arisleus says: I tell you that our master Pythagoras is the foot of the Prophets and the head of the Sages, and that he has received such gifts from God and such wisdom that no one after Hermes <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy.</note> has possessed as much as he. He therefore wished to gather his Disciples, who were sent throughout all regions and provinces, to treat of this precious art <note>The "Great Art" or alchemy, the study of the transmutation of matter and the spirit.</note>, so that their words might serve as a rule for those who come after them. And he commanded that Iximedrus should speak first, who was of very good counsel, who said:

All things have a beginning and a nature, which of itself is sufficient without the help of another to multiply to infinity; otherwise, all would be lost and corrupted.

THE ASSEMBLY <note>original: "LA TOURBE". **BELE** said: You have spoken very well and without envy <note>In alchemical literature, "speaking without envy" means the master is being generous and honest, rather than hiding the truth to spite the student.</note>, God help you, and give grace to the disciples to hear and understand you. **SIRUS** said: You are all envious. Know, sons of doctrine, that the child is begotten of man and woman, and if the two <term>seeds</term><note>The original "spermes" refers to the male and female reproductive fluids; in alchemy, these represent the active (Sulfur) and passive (Mercury) principles.</note> are not joined together, you accomplish nothing. But when the seed of the woman comes to the door of the <term>womb</term><note>original: "matrice"</note>, and meets the seed of the man, they join together: and one is hot and dry, the other cold and moist. And immediately after they have entered, they are mixed, and nature, which governs by the will of God, closes the door of the womb, and they enter into a skin which is within the womb, which is one of the chambers thereof. And the door of the womb and the cell of the said skin where the seeds are located closes so exactly that the woman has no <term>purgations</term><note>Referring to the cessation of the menstrual cycle during pregnancy.</note>, and nothing comes out: therefore the <term>natural heat</term><note>A vital force in medieval physiology believed to drive digestion and development.</note> remains all around the womb, gently digesting the two seeds together.

And the seed of the man does nothing but convert and ripen that of the woman, and then, little by little, the substance that the woman casts out increases the seed and nourishes and fattens it, and is converted by the work of the seed of the man and the natural heat, with the aid of the compound together; it is cooked, and digested, and refined, and purified, until the spirit has movement within this composition. In the first forty days there is movement, and in the following days it turns into milk, then into blood, then into the principal members, and into the formation of the heart and the liver and the other organs. And then the purgations, which were dirty and bloody and black with putrefaction, become white by <term>decoction</term><note>The process of "cooking" or heating a substance to change its state.</note> and are carried white to the breasts, wherewith afterward the child is nourished and suckled until it is grown. And then one gives it to drink all sorts of beverages, and to eat all kinds of meat, and it grows and strengthens with bones, nerves, veins, and blood.

It is the same with our <term>Work</term><note>The "Great Work" (Magnum Opus) is the traditional name for the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> for one who understands it well. And know that although we say in several places, "put this in, put that in"; nevertheless, we mean that it must be put in only once and no more; and then keep it closed until the end, regardless of what we say about "opening and adding": for we do all this in order to lead many astray <note>Alchemical authors frequently admitted to using "decknames" and contradictory instructions to hide their secrets from the uninitiated.</note>. For we do nothing else except provide Nature with the material from which she can work according to her own aim, just as you see in every kind of generation.

First, when we wish to grow a tree, we sow it from its perfect seed which has come from it—for every seed produces fruit similar to that from which it came—and then once we have sown it, we leave it in the earth. There it rots, and then it sprouts a white germ that the earth nourishes; this happens through the active virtue <note>In medieval science, "virtue" refers to an inherent power or life-force.</note> which is inside the rotted seed, and it grows until it becomes a tree like the one it came from. And then from this tree comes another seed which can again multiply to infinity. 

Thus we do nothing but assist the matter, and Nature completes it. Likewise, if a woman goes to several men, she never conceives, and if by chance she does conceive, she brings forth a dead child. For if you mix raw things with cooked things, bad <term>digestion</term> will occur. Therefore, we must have nothing else but the two <term>seeds</term><note>original: "spermes"; these represent the active (Sulfur) and passive (Mercury) principles of the alchemical matter.</note> from one root, and cook them: for they are transformed, provided that you assist them in the manner you ought until the end. Therefore, do this, and leave aside so many words and <term>regimes</term><note>The "regime" refers to the specific stages of heat and the timing required to guide the matter through its transformations.</note>, and watch how Nature acts, and try to imitate her in her governance, and do not be so bold as to wish to do more through your methods than she does:

It is thus with our <term>work</term><note>The "Great Work" (*Magnum Opus*), the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> for whoever understands it well. For we do nothing else except provide nature with the matter from which she herself can work toward her purpose, as you see in all <term>generation</term><note>The natural process of birth, growth, and procreation.</note>. First, when we want to make a tree, we sow it with its perfect seed which came from it, for every seed produces fruit similar to that from which it came; and then when we have sown it, we leave it in the earth. There it rots <note>This refers to *putrefaction*, the first major stage of the alchemical process, where the matter dies and turns black before it can be reborn.</note>, and then sprouts a white germ that the earth nourishes; and this is by the active power that is within the rotted seed, and it grows until it becomes a tree like the one from which it came. And then from this tree comes another seed which can still be multiplied to infinity. Thus, we do nothing but assist the matter, and nature completes it. Also, if a woman goes to many men, she never conceives, and if by chance she does conceive, she brings forth a dead child. For if you mix raw things with cooked things, there will be poor digestion. Therefore, we must have nothing else but the two <term>seeds</term><note>In alchemy, these are the "two sperms" or "metallic seeds"—usually identified as Philosophical Sulfur (the male/active principle) and Philosophical Mercury (the female/passive principle).</note> from one root, and cook them: for they change, provided that you assist them in the manner that you ought until the end. Therefore, do thus, and leave aside so many words and <term>regimens</term><note>The specific methods of applying heat and managing the stages of the alchemical process.</note>, and look at how nature acts, and strive to imitate her in her regimen, and do not be so bold as to wish to do more by your methods than she does:

**LANUS** <note>A speaker in the Turba, sometimes identified as a corruption of a Greek name.</note> says: Know that our work is made of 3, of 4, of 2, and of 1, and the fire is one and is 2, and the colors are three, and the days 7, and 3, and 4, and 1, and understand me. **ACSUB OFFES** <note>Another participant in the Turba discourse; these names are often heavily distorted through centuries of transcription from Arabic to Latin to French.</note> says: Put the red man with his white woman <note>A classic alchemical metaphor for the union of Sulfur (the Red King) and Mercury (the White Queen), or Gold and Silver.</note> in a round house, surrounded by slow heat continually, and leave them there until all is converted into water—not common water, but Philosophical. See black, see white, see red, that is all, for this death is eternal life after the glorious and perfect death.

...surrounded by the heat of a fever, and keep them well in their shell. <note>In alchemy, the "shell" or "egg" refers to the hermetically sealed glass flask—the *Philosophical Egg*—where the transformation takes place.</note> And know that if they begin to change, they complete and beautify themselves on their own: And know that if you prepare this without the correct weight <note>Precision in weight and proportions (the "balance") was considered essential to avoid the explosion of the vessel or the "burning" of the matter.</note>, there will be great delay and great danger of fire, by which delay you will believe you have failed. **MINDIUS** says, Know all you investigators of this art, that the spirit is everything, and that if within this spirit another similar spirit is not enclosed, everything profits nothing. # EXPLANATION OF THE FIGURES

In this book, on the second leaf, he consoled his nation, advising them to flee from vices and above all from Idolatry, waiting with gentle patience for the Messiah to come, who would conquer all the Kings of the earth and reign with his people in eternal glory. Without a doubt, this had been a very learned man.

On the third leaf and in all the other following writings—to help his captive nation pay the tributes to the Roman Emperors, and to do other things that I shall not mention—he taught them <term>metallic transmutation</term> <note>the alchemical process of changing base metals, like lead, into noble metals, like gold</note> in common words. He painted the vessels on the side and gave warning of the colors and everything else, except for the <term>first Agent</term> <note>original: "premier Agent." In alchemy, this is the "Prima Materia," the essential starting substance which was the most closely guarded secret</note>, of which he spoke not at all. But instead, as he said, he painted it and depicted it with great artistry on the fourth and fifth entire leaves. For even though it was very intelligibly depicted and painted, nonetheless no one would have known how to understand it without being well-advanced in their <term>traditional Cabala</term> <note>original: "Cabale traditive," referring to the oral tradition of mystical Jewish knowledge</note> and without having well-studied the books of the *Philosophers* <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers specifically to alchemists</note>. Therefore, the fourth and fifth leaves were without writing, entirely filled with beautiful illuminated figures, or paintings, executed with great skill.

<margin>a 1. Figure of the Jew Abraham</margin>

The first portrait depicted Time, who devours all things; it suggested that a period of six years—corresponding to the six written leaves—was necessary to perfect the Stone. It maintained that after this time, one must turn the hourglass and cook no further. When I told the scholar <note>referring to the scholars Flamel consulted in Paris, mentioned on the previous page</note> that this was only painted to demonstrate and teach the **First Agent** (as was stated in the book), he replied that this six-year decoction was like a second Agent. He argued that the **First Agent** was indeed painted there, being the white and heavy water, which was undoubtedly **Quicksilver** <note>original: "Vif argent"; in alchemy, this refers to Mercury, considered the "womb" or essential fluid of all metals</note>. This Quicksilver could neither be fixed nor have its "feet cut off"—that is to say, have its volatility removed—except by this long cooking in the very pure blood of young children. He claimed that in this blood, the Quicksilver, joining with Gold and Silver, would first be converted with them into a **Herb** similar to the one painted; then, after corruption, into **Serpents**, which, once entirely dried and cooked by fire, would be reduced to a powder of gold, which would be the **Stone**.

This was the reason that, during the long space of twenty-one years, I made a thousand errors and muddles—though never with real blood, which is a wicked and villainous thing. For I found in my book that the Philosophers called "blood" the *mineral spirit* which is within the metals, principally within the *Sun* (Gold), the *Moon* (Silver), and *Mercury*, toward the assembly of which I always aimed. Furthermore, these interpretations were for the most part more clever than they were true. Therefore, never seeing the signs in my operations at the times written in my book, I was always starting over. Finally, having lost all hope of ever understanding these Figures, I made a vow to God and to **St. James of Galicia** <note>Saint James the Greater, whose shrine at Santiago de Compostela in Spain was, and is, a major pilgrimage site</note> to seek their interpretation from some Jewish Priest in one of the Synagogues of Spain.

## Theological [Interpretations], which may be given to these Hieroglyphics according to my understanding.

### CHAPTER I.

I have given to this Cemetery a <term>charnel house</term> <note>A building where bones unearthed from graves were stored to make room for new burials; Flamel famously funded such structures at the Holy Innocents' Cemetery.</note> which is opposite this fourth arch, with the Cemetery in the middle; and against one of the pillars of this charnel house, I have had sketched and roughly painted a man all in black who looks at these <term>Hieroglyphics</term> <note>Flamel uses this term to refer to his symbolic alchemical illustrations.</note>, around whom is written in French: *I see a marvel at which I am greatly amazed.* <note>original: "Je voy merveille dont moult je m’ébahis." **Flamel**. For these **Vessels** mean nothing else than that I have performed the <term>magistery</term> <note>The "Great Work" (Magnum Opus) or the successful completion of the alchemical process to create the Philosopher's Stone.</note> three times in similar ones. The theological sense is also understood well enough by this writing; one must only speak of the rest which is above it.

The **two dragons** united, one inside the other, of a black and blue color, in a <term>field of sable</term> <note>In the language of heraldry, "sable" refers to the color black.</note>—that is to say, black—of which one has golden wings and the other has none, are the **sins** which naturally support one another; for one is born of the other. Of these sins, some can be driven away easily, as they come easily, for they fly toward us at every hour. But those that have no wings cannot be driven away, such as is the **sin against the Holy Spirit**. This **gold of the wings** signifies that most of these sins come from the <term>sacred hunger for gold</term> <note>A reference to the Latin phrase *auri sacra fames*, denoting an insatiable and accursed greed for wealth.</note>, which makes so many people attentive, and which makes them think so intently about where they can get some. And the black and blue color demonstrates that these are desires that emerge from the dark pit of hell, which we must entirely flee. These two dragons can also represent, morally, the legions of evil spirits...

## *The Philosophical Interpretations according to the Mastery of Hermes.*

### CHAPTER II.

I desire with all my heart that he who seeks this secret of the Sages, having turned over in his mind these ideas of the life and future resurrection, should first make his profit from them. The Philosopher never smells this stench unless he breaks his Vessels <term>Vessels: The airtight glass containers holding the alchemical work.</term>, but only judges it to be such by the sight and the changing of colors, which come from the rot of his ***confections*** <term>Confections: The specific mixtures or medicinal preparations of substances within the alchemical process.</term>.

These colors, then, signify the ***putrefaction*** and ***generation*** <note>In alchemy, "generation" refers to the birth of a new substance out of the "death" or decomposition of the old.</note> given to us by the biting and dissolution of our perfect bodies. The color you must have must be entirely perfect in blackness, similar to that of these Dragons, and this within the space of forty days.

Therefore, let those who do not have these essential signs withdraw early from their operations, so that they may avoid a certain loss. Know also and note well, that in this Art, it is nothing to have blackness; there is nothing easier to obtain. For from almost all things in the world mixed with moisture, you will obtain blackness through fire. You must have a blackness that comes from perfect metallic bodies, which lasts for a long period of time, and is only lost after five months, after which the desired whiteness arrives and follows. As for the bluish and yellowish color, it signifies that the *solution* and *putrefaction* are not yet finished, and that the colors of our *Mercury* <term>Mercury (Mercure): In alchemy, this is not just the liquid metal, but the "philosophical spirit" or the feminine, receptive principle of the work.</term> are not yet well mixed and rotted with what remains.

This refers to the tiny dust motes visible only when dancing in a beam of sunlight.</note>, which are afterwards changed into *Permanent Water* <term>Permanent Water (Eau permanente): A stable, non-evaporating liquid produced during the process, symbolizing the soul of the matter.</term>. And this *dissolution* is called by the envious Philosophers <note>Alchemical authors often called themselves "envious" because they intentionally obscured their writings to prevent the "unworthy" from succeeding.</note> *Death*, *Destruction*, and *Perdition*, because the natures change their form. From this have come so many allegories about the dead, tombs, and sepulchers. Others have named it *Calcination*, *Denudation*, *Separation*, *Trituration*, and *Assation*, because the confections are changed and reduced into very small pieces or parts. Others call it *Reduction to the first matter*, *Mollification*, *Extraction*, *Commixtion*, *Liquefaction*, *Conversion of Elements*, *Subtiliation*, *Division*, *Humation*, *Impastation*, and *Distillation*, because the confections are liquefied, reduced to seed, softened, and circulate within the vessel.

### OF NICOLAS FLAMEL.

A King most powerful, invincible, and incorruptible, because he shall be an admirable <term>quintessence</term> <note>The 'fifth element' or quintessence was believed to be the pure, celestial essence of matter, existing beyond the four earthly elements of earth, air, fire, and water.</note>. The second part, which is also very notable, is that I had to depict two bodies, because in this operation you must divide that which has been <term>coagulated</term>, in order to later provide nourishment—a milk of life—to the little newborn child, who is endowed (by the living God) with a <term>vegetative soul</term> <note>In alchemical theory, the 'vegetative soul' refers to the basic life force that allows matter to 'grow' and transform within the vessel, much like a plant.</note>. This is a most admirable and hidden secret which has driven mad all those who sought it without finding it, for lack of understanding; yet it has made wise every person who has contemplated it with the eyes of the body or the spirit.

You must therefore make two parts and portions of this coagulated body, one of which will serve as <term>Azoth</term> <note>original: "Azoth"; This refers to the universal solvent or the 'Mercury of the Philosophers,' essential for the purification of the matter.</note> to wash and purify the other, which is called <term>Leton</term> <note>original: "Leton"; Also known as Laton or Latona, this represents the impure 'black' matter that must be cleansed until it becomes white.</note>, which must be whitened. That which is washed is the **Serpent Python**, who, having taken his being from the corruption of the slime of the earth gathered by the waters of the deluge—when all the mixtures were water—must be put to death and conquered by the arrows of the God **Apollo**, by the fair **Sun**, that is to say, by our fire which is equal to that of the Sun.

The one who washes—or rather, these washings, which must be continued with the other half—are the teeth of this Serpent, which the wise operator, the valiant **Theseus**, shall sow in the same earth. From these shall be born Soldiers who will finally destroy themselves, allowing themselves by their positioning to be resolved into the same nature as the earth, leaving behind the deserved conquests <note>Flamel here combines various myths; the sowing of dragon teeth is usually attributed to Cadmus or Jason, but here he uses Theseus to represent the 'valiant' alchemist who manages the volatile reactions of the work.</note>.

It is upon this that the Philosophers have written so often, and so many times repeated: *It dissolves* <note>original: "Il se dissout"</note>
