# CHAPTER VIII.

### EXPLANATION OF THIS FIGURE.

<margin>Figure 6.</margin>
This violet and blue field shows that, desiring to pass from the White Stone to the Red, you have soaked it with a little <term>Solar Virgin's Milk: a symbolic term for a specific alchemical solvent or "mercury" used to nourish the stone</term>, and that these colors have emerged from the <term>Mercurial moisture: the fluid or "spirit" within the chemical mixture</term> that you have dried upon the Stone. In this operation of <term>rubefaction: the final stage of the Great Work, characterized by the color red</term>, even though you soak it, you will have hardly any blackness, but rather much violet, blue, and the color of the <term>peacock's tail: the "Cauda Pavonis," a stage where many iridescent colors appear as the matter dries</term>: for our Stone is so triumphant in dryness that as soon as your Mercury touches it, nature—rejoicing in its own nature—joins with it and drinks it greedily; and therefore the blackness that comes from moisture can only show itself a little, beneath these violet and blue colors, since dryness (as has been said) now governs absolutely.

And truly, I tell you a secret here that you will very rarely find written. <margin>a Open, Close, Dissolve, Bind. <note>original: "Aperì Clause Solve Liga"</note></margin>
To show you even more that she asks for multiplication, I have had the man to whom she makes her prayer painted in the form of a Saint Peter, holding a key, having the power to open and close, to bind and loosen. This is because the <term>envious Philosophers: historical alchemists who intentionally hid their secrets from the uninitiated</term> have never spoken of Multiplication except under these common terms of the art: *Open, close, bind, and loosen*. They called *opening and loosening* the act of making the body (which is always hard and <term>fixed: resistant to heat; solid</term>) soft, fluid, and flowing like water; and *closing or binding* meant to <term>coagulate: to thicken or solidify</term> it afterward by a stronger <term>decoction: prolonged heating or boiling</term>, returning it once more to the form of a body.

It was therefore necessary for me to represent a man with a key, to teach you that you must now *open and close*—that is to say, multiply—the germinating and growing natures. For as many times as you shall dissolve and fix, so many times will these natures multiply in quantity, quality, and virtue, according to the multiplication of ten; this number coming to a hundred, from a hundred to a thousand, from a thousand to ten thousand, from ten thousand to a hundred thousand, from a hundred thousand to a million; and from there by the same operation until infinity, as I have done three times, for which I praise God. And when your <term>Elixir: the completed Stone in liquid or powder form</term> is thus led to infinity, one grain of it falling upon a molten metallic quantity as deep and vast as the Ocean will <term>tinge: to dye or transform the inner nature of a metal</term> and convert it into very perfect metal, that is to say, into Silver or into Gold, according as it has been <term>imbibed: soaked in alchemical liquids</term> and fermented, chasing and driving away from it all the...

In the first, I wish to speak of the Inventors of this worthy Science, and of the Sages who possessed it, how and according to what I have known.

In the second Part, I shall speak of myself, of my time, and how from the beginning until the end I came to know it, and how I performed everything and everywhere, without any envy <note>original: "envie" — In alchemical literature, "envy" refers to the practice of "Hermetic secrecy," where authors deliberately obscured their writings to prevent the unworthy from succeeding</note>, the labors I endured in pursuing it.

In the third Part, I wish to speak of the principles and roots of Metals, and present clear and philosophical reasons.

In the fourth Part of my book, I wish to speak of the practice, which I shall present somewhat <term>Parabolically: Described through parables, allegories, or metaphors rather than literal chemical instructions</term>; but not so much that, by applying yourself, you will not understand it well.

And through the other Parts you may be marvelously instructed: And if you do not understand the work through my book, truly I believe that you will never arrive at this Art. But do not think to understand it on the second, nor the third time, nor the tenth time; but rather to always understand it more by repeating it: And I say nothing in my book that I do not prove by clear reasons and experiences, and also by the authority of the Masters speaking in this Art and Science most reasonably and with great logic.

how then do you expect them to become the Stone—which is a noble intermediate form between Metal and <term>Quicksilver: or Mercury; the fluid spirit believed to be the root of all metals</term>—if that [metallic] form is not first taken away and corrupted? And for this reason, Aristotle and Democritus say in the Book of Physics, in the 3rd Chapter of the *Meteorology* <note>original: "Metheores"; referring to Aristotle's *Meteorologica*. But the ignorant think they understand this phrase—"reduction to the first matter"—in this way: namely, to reduce it, as they say, into the four Elements. For the four Elements make up the first matter of created things. They speak the truth when they say the first matter consists of the four Elements; but that is to say, they make up the first matter *of* the first matter. That is to say, all four Elements are the things from which <term>Sulfur: the active, "combustible" principle in alchemy</term> and Quicksilver are made, which [in turn] make up the <term>First Matter: the primal, formless substance from which a specific class of things (like metals) originates</term> of Metals. The reason why is this: the four Elements are just as good for making a Donkey or an Ox as they are for making Metals. For nature must first turn the Elements into Quicksilver and Sulfur before the Elements can be called the "first matter" of Metals. Just as, for example, when a man is composed, he is not composed of the four Elements while they are still [raw] elements; rather, nature has already transmuted them into the first matter of man. <meta>This page continues the argument from page 118, where the author clarifies that the "reduction to first matter" required for alchemy does not mean returning a metal to the four basic elements (Earth, Air, Fire, Water), but rather to its specific metallic origins: Sulfur and Mercury.</meta>

nature has transmuted the four Elements into <term>Mercury: the fluid, "feminine" principle of metals</term> and <term>Sulfur: the active, "masculine" principle of metals</term>; only then is it the proper first matter of Metals. Why? Because whatever Nature does afterwards with this matter—that is to say, Mercury and Sulfur—it will always result in a Metallic form. But before and during the time they were still the four Elements, and when it was not yet Quicksilver nor Sulfur, Nature could very well have made from those four Elements an Ox, a Herb, or a Man, or some other thing. Thus it appears clearly that the four Elements, which they <note>Referring to the "ignorant" or mistaken alchemists mentioned on the previous page.</note> speak of, do not constitute the first matter of Metals; rather, *Sulfur and Quicksilver are called the proper and true first matter of Metals*. And if what they said were true, it would follow that Men, metals, herbs, plants, and brute beasts would all be one and the same thing, and there would be no difference between them. For if that were true, Metals would be nothing but the four Elements; and thus everything would be one single thing, which would be to grant a great absurdity <note>original: "un grand inconvenient"; in the logic of the time, this refers to a fundamental contradiction that would break the laws of nature.</note>. And so it appears clearly that the four Elements, remaining as they are, do not make up the first matter of Metals.

I wish to prove it further in this way: for if it were true that the four Elements were the first matter of Metals, it would follow that Men could be made from Metals, for Men are made of nothing but the four Elements. And so it would follow that from one thing, any other thing could be made, and like would not beget its like—any more than the metal would—for everything would be nothing but the four Elements. # THIRD PART

## Wherein the principles and roots of Metals are treated, through evident and philosophical reasoning.

To have an understanding of this matter, one must first know that, in the beginning, God made a confused and disordered matter without any structure, which was full, by the will of God, of many substances. And from this matter, He drew the four Elements, from which He made various beasts and creatures by mixing them. Some creatures He made **Intellectual** <term>Intellectual: "Intellectives," referring to humans, who possess a rational soul capable of logic and divine contemplation</term>, others **Sensitive** <term>Sensitive: "Sensitives," referring to animals, which possess senses and movement but lacks human reason</term>, others **Vegetative** <term>Vegetative: "Vegetatives," referring to plants, which possess the power of growth and nutrition but lack senses</term>, and others **Mineral**. 

The **Intellectual** and **Sensitive** creatures are created from the four Elements; however, fire and air have more dominance in them than the others. Nevertheless, in the **Sensitive** creatures, fire is lowered in power, because air is just as much a lord in that state as fire is—as seen in the brute Beasts, Horses, Donkeys, Birds, and all Sensitive Creatures. 

The others are created from the four Elements and are called **Vegetative Creatures**, which grow and nourish themselves and have life; but they have no senses, nor understanding. These are composed of air and water, which hold dominance there; but here, the air is already lowered from its dignity by the water, and the water is lowered by a single vaporous earthly substance. 

And thus following these are the **Minerals**, which are created from earth and water; but the dignity of the water is more earthy than it is aquatic. And in these Minerals, there are various for— <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely "formes" (forms), continuing on the next page.</note>

1. The first is **Lead**, the least hot and moist.

For if it were so, the matter of Metals would not be of a homogeneous <term>Homogeneous: In alchemy, this refers to a substance made of a single, unified nature rather than a mixture of different things</term> nature, which goes against the teachings of all the Philosophers. But the Philosophers called this "Sulfur" because, in its dominant qualities, it is an inflammable thing, like sulfur; hot and dry, like sulfur. And because of this similarity, it is called sulfur; but it is not common sulfur, as some fools believe.

Thus you can clearly see that the metallic form is created by nature from nothing other than pure Mercurial substance, and not from any foreign material.

But the plain natural path, as I have already told and declared to you in my <term>Speculative</term> <note>The "Speculative" refers to the theoretical portion of alchemical study, as opposed to the "Practical" laboratory work.</note>.

For through my Book I pray truly enough for your bodies and for your goods; provided that you believe it without error, and flee from those who wander and their opinions, as well as their company. For you could not imagine the damage that can come to you from such total deviation.

Let such and similar slanderers cease from now on; I wish to warn them not to trouble themselves with the reading of my present **Little Treatise** <term>Opuscule</term>: For it is not for them that I have composed it; but for the **benevolent Children** <term>Enfans benevoles</term> <note>A traditional term for dedicated students or "Sons of Art" who are spiritually and intellectually prepared for alchemical study.</note>, the teachable, and the lovers of our Science. These I pray most humbly that, before they set themselves to work, they have resolved in their understandings each and every operation necessary for the composition of our **Divine Work** <term>divine Oeuvre</term>, and have adapted these so well to the sayings, contradictions, riddles, and ambiguities found in the Books of the Philosophers, that they no longer perceive any contradiction or variety whatsoever. For that is the true means to know the truth, and principally of this **Divine Philosophy** <term>divine Philosophie</term>, as **Rasis** <note>Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi (865–925), a Persian polymath and alchemist.</note> writes much better, saying: *He who is lazy in reading our Books will never be quick to prepare the materials. For one of the Books explains another, and what is missing in one is added in another.* Because one must never expect (and this by Divine judgment) to find the full accomplishment of our **Divine Work** written and declared...

<summary>Denis Zachaire argues that alchemy is a "Divine" science that transcends simple natural philosophy and warns skeptics to avoid his book. He advises serious students to resolve the contradictions in philosophical texts by cross-referencing different authors before beginning practical work.</summary>

### LITTLE TREATISE

in order; just as Aristotle wrote very well to King Alexander, responding to his request. *It is not lawful,* he said, *to ask for something that it is not permitted to grant. How then do you think that I should write at length on paper that which the hearts of men could not bear if it were set down in writing?* <note>Zachaire refers here to a legendary correspondence between Aristotle and Alexander the Great, a common theme in medieval and Renaissance alchemy where philosophers claimed that their secrets were too powerful or sacred to be written plainly.</note> Giving to understand well enough by the refusal he made to the King, his Master, that it is forbidden, by Divine ordinance, to publish our **Science** <term>Science</term> <note>In alchemical texts, "Science" or "The Art" refers specifically to the secret knowledge of transmutation and the creation of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> in terms such as would be understood by the common people.

Wherefore I adjure by these presents all those who, by means of my present **Little Treatise** <term>Opuscule</term>, shall arrive at the true knowledge of this **Divine Work** <term>divine Oeuvre</term>; that they handle it in such a way that the poor may be fed by it, the oppressed relieved of their troubles, and the weary comforted for the love of our good God, who will have shared such a great good with them; of whom I pray them once more to recognize the whole, and as coming from Him, to use it according to His holy Commandments. Doing this, He will cause them to prosper in their affairs, just as, on the contrary, He will permit everything to lead to their confusion.

I beseech you therefore, faithful Friend, that in reading our Books, you always have this good God in your understanding, because all good descends from Him, and without His help, there is nothing perfect in this low world; much less can one arrive at the knowledge of this great and admirable good, if His **Holy Spirit** <note>The "Holy Spirit" here represents the internal illumination or divine grace that alchemists believed was necessary to decode the "blind" or metaphorical language of hermetic texts.</note> is not given to us as a guide. As in truth He will do, if avarice does not lead you, and if you are a true zealot of **JESUS CHRIST**; to whom be glorious praise for ages of ages. Amen.

# FIRST PART.

### *How the Author arrived at the knowledge of this divine Work.*

Hermes, rightly called Trismegistus <note>original: "Trismegiste." From the Greek *Trismegistos*, meaning "Thrice-Great," a legendary figure to whom many foundational alchemical and hermetic texts were attributed.</note> (which is commonly interpreted as **Thrice-Great**), Author and first Prophet of the natural Philosophers, after having seen through experience the certainty and truth of this divine Philosophy, has very well and with good reason left in writing, that had it not been for the fear he had of the universal Judgment, which the Sovereign God must make of all rational creatures in the last days of the world’s consummation, he would never have left anything in writing of this divine Science <term>Science</term> <note>In this context, "Science" refers to the "Sacred Art" or Alchemy—the pursuit of the Philosopher’s Stone and the understanding of nature’s hidden laws.</note>, so much did he esteem it—and with just cause—as great and admirable. In this opinion were all the principal authors who followed him. This is the reason why they have all written their Books in such a way, as Geber <note>Geber refers to Jābir ibn Hayyān, an 8th-century polymath, though here the author likely refers to the "Latin Geber," a 13th-century writer whose *Summa Perfectionis* was a cornerstone of alchemical study.</note> says in his *Summa* <note>original: "Somme." A reference to the *Summa Perfectionis Magisterii* (The Sum of the Perfection of Mastery), one of the most influential medieval alchemical texts.</note>, that they always conclude in two parts, in order to make the ignorant fail, and to declare, beneath this variety of opinions, their principal intention to the **Children of Science** <note>A traditional term for dedicated students of alchemy who are deemed spiritually and intellectually worthy of the secret.</note>. It is fitting that these students err at the beginning; so that, they say, having acquired it with great pain and labor of body and understanding, they might hold it more dear and more secret. Which, in truth, is a great reason not to publish it at all, because an unspeakable trouble is required to acquire it, without counting the costs and expenses which are very great, before being able to arrive at the perfect knowledge of this divine Work— <note>The text breaks here mid-sentence, transitioning to the next page.</note>

He explains that this secrecy ensures that only those who are truly dedicated and "worthy" can uncover the secrets of the Art.</summary>

...we bought three marks <note>A unit of weight for precious metals, roughly 244 grams.</note> of silver, and had them filed down; from these he made small **Nails** <note>The original French "Clouds" is an archaic spelling of "clous" (nails).</note> using an artificial paste. He then mixed them with pulverized **Cinnabar** <term>Cinnabar</term> <note>Mercury sulfide; a bright red mineral which alchemists frequently used in attempts to create mercury or gold.</note>, and then cooked them in a well-covered earthen vessel for a certain time. When they were quite dry, he melted them or passed them through the **cupel** <term>cupelle</term> <note>A small, porous bowl used in assaying to separate precious metals from lead and other impurities.</note>; the result was that we found three marks and a little bit more of fine Silver, which he claimed had come out of the Cinnabar, and that the fine silver we had originally put in had "flown away in smoke." Whether there was any profit, God knows—and so do I, who spent more than thirty crowns on it; nonetheless, he constantly maintained that there was a gain. This became so well known in Paris before the following Christmas that there was no "son of a good mother" <note>An idiom for a respectable or well-intentioned person.</note> dabbling in the **Science** (that is to say, in **sophistications** <term>sophistications</term> <note>In the 16th century, this referred to deceptive or fraudulent alchemical methods, such as making alloys that looked like gold but were not.</note>) who did not know of or had not heard talk of the **Nails of Cinnabar**; just as some time later, there was talk of **Apples of Copper**, used to fix **Mercury** therein with the **Moon** <note>In alchemical symbolism, "the Moon" (Luna) refers to Silver.</note>.

While these youthful follies were passing, a foreign Gentleman arrived who was highly expert in Sophistications—so much so that he regularly made a profit from them and sold his work to Goldsmiths. I joined his company as soon as I possibly could. However, this was not without spending money, so that he would not think me needy. I remained nearly a year in his company before he was willing to reveal anything to me. Finally, he showed me his secret, which he esteemed very highly, though in truth it was far from perfect.

Meanwhile, I informed my Abbot of everything I had been able to do, and even sent him a copy of the instructions for the aforementioned Gentleman's practice. He...

This answer was so tiresome to me that, without waiting for his fine promises, I returned to the Abbot.

But because I had heard tell of a Religious Doctor <note>likely a monk or friar with a doctoral degree</note> who was esteemed (and rightly so) as learned in **Natural Philosophy** <term>Natural Philosophy: the historical study of nature and the physical universe, the precursor to modern science</term>, I wished to go see him on my way back; he greatly turned me away from all these **Sophistications** <term>Sophistications: in alchemy, this refers to fraudulent or deceptive methods used to imitate gold or silver rather than truly transforming metals</term>. I spoke to him of the work I had done, but he knew very well how to tell me what it was, and that it would not withstand many tests <note>original: "essais"; referring to metallurgical assays used to test the purity of gold or silver</note>. ...I studied, then I would almost entirely change my mind; waiting until I could form an opinion where there was no variety or contradiction to the **Sentences** <note>In this context, 'sentences' refers to the authoritative opinions or maxims of the philosophers</note> in the books of the Philosophers. Being in this perplexity, I returned to frequenting those I knew worked at this divine Work: For I no longer associated with all the other **Operators** <note>The manual practitioners of alchemy</note> I had known before, who worked at those cursed **Sophistications** <term>Sophistications: Fraudulent chemical techniques used to create deceptive imitations of precious metals</term>. But if I had conflict in my understanding coming out of my study, it was only increased by considering the diverse and variable ways in which they worked; for if one worked with gold alone, the other with gold and **Mercury** together, another mixed in lead which he called "sounding lead," because it had passed through the **retort** <note>A glass vessel with a long downward-pointing neck used for distillation</note> with **quicksilver** <note>An archaic name for Mercury</note>. Another converted certain metals into quicksilver, using a variety of **simples** <note>Individual chemical or medicinal ingredients</note> through sublimations. The other worked with an artificial black **atrament** <term>Atrament: A term for various black substances, often iron or copper sulfates (vitriol), used as a base for chemical reactions</term>, which he said was the true matter that **Raymond Lulle** <note>Raymond Lully (c. 1232–1315), a major figure in medieval alchemy and philosophy</note> used for the composition of this **Great Work**. If one worked in an **alembic** <term>Alembic: A distillation apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube</term>, the other worked in several others, and various glass vessels, another in brass, another in copper, another in lead, another in silver, and some even in a vessel of gold. Then one performed his **decoction** <note>The process of heating a substance to extract its essence or transform it</note> using a fire made of large coals, another of wood, another of grape seeds, another from the heat of the sun, and others in a **bain-marie** <term>Bain-marie: A water bath used to provide gentle, even heat to a vessel</term>.

[to] review with great diligence the Works of Ramon Llull <note>Raymond Lulle: A Majorcan philosopher and polymath (c. 1232–1315). While he likely did not practice alchemy, a massive body of alchemical literature was attributed to him in the centuries following his death.</note>, and especially his **Testament** and **Codicil**, which I adapted so well with an Epistle that he wrote in his time to King Robert <note>Robert of Anjou (1277–1343), King of Naples, a frequent addressee in pseudo-Lullian alchemical works.</note>, and a rough draft that I had recovered from the said Doctor <note>Referring to Llull, often called the *Doctor Illuminatus*</note>, which was useless to him; that I formed from them a **resolution** <term>Resolution: Here meaning a firm theoretical conclusion or a proven chemical path</term> entirely contrary to all the Operations that I had seen before; but such that I read nothing in all the books that did not adapt itself very well to my opinion, especially the resolution that Arnaldus de Villa Nova <note>A famous 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> made at the heart of his *Grand Rosary*, who was the Master of Ramon Llull in this science. So much so that I remained about a year afterward, doing nothing else but reading and thinking about my resolution day and night; while waiting for the term of the lease <note>original: "l'assensement," a legal arrangement for the management of his property</note> I had made of my estate to pass, so I could go work at my own home. I arrived there at the beginning of **Lent**, determined to practice my said resolution; during which time I made provision for everything I needed and set up a furnace to work; so that on the day after **Easter**, I began.

But this was not without having various hindrances (of which I remain silent on the principal ones) from my closest neighbors, relatives, and friends. One said to me, "What do you want to do? Have you not already spent enough on such follies?" Another assured me that if I continued to buy so much small charcoal <note>Charcoal was the essential fuel for alchemical furnaces; large purchases often drew unwanted attention from the authorities</note>, they would suspect me of making **counterfeit money**, as he had already heard talk of it. Then came another, telling me that everyone, even the most prominent of our town, found it very strange that I did not practice the profession of the **long robe** <note>The "robe longue" refers to the legal or judicial profession</note>, considering that I was a **Licentiate of Laws** <term>Licentiate of Laws: A person who has earned a degree allowing them to practice law</term>, to par-

<page-num>172</page-num>
<header>### LITTLE TREATISE</header>

I was glad, God knows. Yet I did not boast of it for all that; but after having given thanks to our good God, who had shown me so much favor and grace through his Son and our Redeemer **JESUS CHRIST**, and having prayed that He would illuminate me by His **Holy Spirit**, so that I might be able to use it for His honor and praise; I set off the next day to find the **Abbot** in his **Abbey**, to fulfill the faith and promise <note>A mutual oath of secrecy and shared success often made between alchemical "partners" or seekers.</note> that we had made together; but I found that he had been dead for six months, for which I was greatly saddened. I also learned of the death of the good **Doctor**, of which I was informed while passing near his **Convent**. Therefore I went to a certain place to wait there for a friend of mine, and a close relative, just as we had agreed together at my departure, whom I had left at my house with a power of attorney <term>procure: a legal document authorizing someone to act on another's behalf</term> and express charge to sell each and every one of my paternal goods that I possessed, from which he paid my **creditors**, and distributed the rest secretly to those who were in need; so that my **Parents** and others might feel some fruit of the great wealth that God had given me, without anyone taking notice. But on the contrary, they thought that I, as one in despair and ashamed of the foolish expenses I had made, was selling my property to retire elsewhere; just as this friend of mine reported to me. He came to find me on the first day of the month of July, and we went to **Lausanne**, having decided to travel and spend the rest of my days in a certain and most renowned city of **Germany**, with a very small retinue <note>original: "petit train," meaning a modest traveling party of servants and horses to avoid drawing attention to his new wealth.</note>; so that I should not be known, even by those who see and read this book of mine during my life in our country of **France**, which I wished to gratify with it; not to be the Author of so many foolish expenses that are usually...

### Containing the true method for reading the books of the Natural Philosophers. <note>In the Renaissance, "Natural Philosophers" referred to those who studied the physical world and its laws, including what we now call scientists and alchemists.</note>

## PART II.

### Regarding the Certainty and Truth of this Science.

But following the order we have begun, it is necessary to explain the second part of our division, namely how our Science is certain and true. However, before beginning, I must satisfy the delicate ears of the Slanderers, who, being accustomed to criticizing the labors of others (because their own never see the light of day), will say that I have poorly remembered the Doctrine of **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle's *Physics* was a foundational text for medieval and Renaissance science, though the specific reference here to the "7th Book" regarding definitions is Zachaire’s application of Aristotelian logic to alchemical theory.</note>, who wrote in the 7th Book of his *Physics* that the definition is the true form of the defined subject. But I will gladly refer them to the Authors who preceded us; who, having put themselves to the task of providing a certain definition, were forced to confess that it is impossible to give one; as the writings of **Morien** <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary 7th-century hermit said to have taught alchemy to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note>, the ***Lilium*** <note>The *Lilium Intelligentiae* (Lily of Intelligence), a text also mentioned on the previous page.</note>, and many others testify. For this reason, they have assigned various and varying descriptions in their books, through which they show the effects of our Science; because it does not have familiar principles, as all other Sciences do.

## SECTION II.

### *On the certainty and truth of the Science.*

But following our established order, we must declare the second Section of our division: namely, how our Science is certain and true. However, before beginning, I must satisfy the delicate ears of the Critics, who—being accustomed to rebuking the labors of others (because their own labors never see the light of day)—will say that I have poorly remembered the Doctrine of **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle (384–322 BC). His *Physics* was the foundational text for understanding matter and change in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note>, who wrote in the 7th Book of his *Physics* that the definition is the true form of the defined subject. And thus, since I have undertaken to provide the declaration and true method of this Science (commonly called **Alchemy** <term>Alchemy: Zachaire uses "Chimie" and "Alchimie" interchangeably here, as was common before the two fields were formally separated.</term>), I ought to have begun with its Definition, the better to declare the property of its terms.

But I will gladly refer them to the Authors who preceded us; who, having set themselves the task of providing a certain definition, were forced to confess that it is impossible to give one, as the writings of **Morienus** <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist who allegedly taught the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note>, the ***Lily*** <note>Referring to the *Lilium Alchimiae*, a widely-circulated alchemical text often attributed to Arnald of Villanova.</note>, and several others testify. For this reason, they have assigned various and differing descriptions in their books, through which they show the effects of our Science; this is because it possesses no familiar principles <note>In the scholastic sense, "familiar principles" are self-evident starting points or axioms used in other sciences like geometry or logic.</note> as all other Sciences do.

For my part, I will say what it seems to me to be. It is, <gloss>Definition of Alchemy.</gloss> then, a part of **Natural Philosophy**, which demonstrates the way to perfect **Metals** on earth, imitating Nature in its operations as closely as is possible for it. Which Science [leads] us...

we declare it to be certain for many reasons.

1. First, it is completely resolved among all the Philosophers that there is nothing more certain than the truth; which, as **Aristotle** says, appears where there is no contradiction. For all those who have written of it agree in this: that there is but one single way to perfect it.

# OPUSCULE

This small treatise <term>Opuscule: A small book or literary work.</term> could not possibly contain every argument that could be made on this subject, yet those already provided should be quite sufficient to demonstrate the truth and certainty of our Science <term>Science: Here referring specifically to Alchemy, often called the "Sacred Science."</term>. Were it not for the arguments usually made to the contrary, which so trouble the understanding of the good Children of the Doctrine <note>A traditional term for dedicated students or initiates of alchemical secrets.</note> that they are always in doubt, believing now one thing and then another, so much so that they never have peace in their minds. But so that they may henceforth believe our Science to be most true, I wish to teach them the true solution to the most forceful and apparent argument usually made against us. By this, they shall know that their arguments, and all others like them, possess nothing but a mere appearance of truth.

They are all accustomed to making an argument which they base on the authority of the Philosopher <note>Aristotle was almost universally referred to as "The Philosopher" in medieval and Renaissance scholarly texts.</note>, in the fourth book of the *Meteorologica* <note>Aristotle’s *Meteorologica* was the standard text for understanding the physical world; its fourth book was considered the foundation of mineralogy.</note>, which was likewise held by Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath (980–1037) whose works on medicine and chemistry were foundational in Europe.</note>, as Albert the Great <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and bishop who sought to reconcile Aristotelian philosophy with Christian faith and alchemy.</note> says. *In vain,* he says, *do the operators of today labor to perfect the Metals, for they will never succeed if they do not first reduce them to their first matter.* <note>original: "En vain... se travaillent les Operateurs... si premierement ils ne les reduisent en leur premiere matiere." This refers to a famous dictum often cited to debunk alchemy: the idea that you cannot turn lead into gold unless you first break the lead down into the universal "prime matter" (*materia prima*) from which all things are made.</note> Now, it is argued that we do not reduce them to this state; consequently, we perform nothing but Sophistications <term>Sophistications: Fraudulent imitations or "faked" gold and silver that only look real on the surface.</term>, as the same Albert has written, saying: *All those who color the Metals, by various ways using simples <term>simples: Single, uncompounded ingredients, often botanical or mineral, used in their natural state.</term>, into various colors, are truly deceivers and tricksters, unless they reduce them to their first matter.*

For my part, I know well that many learned people have undertaken the solution to this argument, because it is the most impressive one that can be made. Thus, some say that even though by the projection <term>projection: The final act of the alchemical process, where the "Philosopher's Stone" is cast upon base metal to transform it into gold.</term> of our divine Work upon imperfect metals, we do not reduce them...

<header>TREATISE</header>

**Work** <term>Work: Usually refers to the "Great Work" (*Magnum Opus*), the successful creation of the Philosopher's Stone or the Elixir.</term>, so that they may be perfected by its great and exuberant perfection: there is no need to reduce them to their prime matter. Therefore, in continuing the order of my division, I shall declare the third part of it, showing which operations are necessary for the making of our **Divine Work**, declaring first how our **Science** <term>Science: In the 16th century, "science" referred to a systematic body of knowledge or an art based on principles, rather than the modern experimental method.</term> is natural, and why it is called Divine. To well understand, then, in what way our science is natural, we must know what **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle's theories on the composition of minerals from "exhalations" remained the standard scientific framework for alchemy during the Renaissance.</note> taught concerning the operations of **Nature**. <header>TRACT</header>

Now, the reason why our **Science** is useless without the said **Conjunction**, is that at the birth and procreation of our **Divine Work**, the volatile part carries away the fixed part with it; and thus we would not know how to ensure that it remained fixed and permanent in the fire, if we did not—by an admirable (even supernatural) **Conjunction**—make the fixed part retain the volatile. ->*How Nature works in the Mines to create Metals.*<-

<header>OF D. ZACHAIRE.</header>

(who has more closely investigated the causes in the procreation of Metals than any other) shows very well that this watery moisture is not the common moisture that we see in water and in other simple substances. For experience shows us that common moisture is reduced and converted into smoke <note>In early chemistry, "smoke" or "fume" often refers to what we would now call vapor or gas produced by evaporation.</note> by the violence of fire. But it is the case that metals, being melted, are not converted into smoke. It must therefore be said that their moisture is mixed with some other matter which retains them in the fire, and which prevents them from being converted into smoke by its violence. Now, there is no matter that resists fire as much as viscous moisture does, when it is mixed with the earthy and subtle part; as Bonus, an *Italian* Philosopher, <note>Petrus Bonus of Ferrara was a 14th-century physician and alchemist, best known for his work "The Precious New Pearl" (*Pretiosa Margarita Novella*).</note> testifies, and as experience certifies to us. Wherefore, it must be said that the moisture which is in Metals is such.

But because we see that there are moistures in them which are consumed by the fire, without the metals themselves being consumed for it—as experience shows us in their purifications—it is necessary for us to confess, with the principal Authors of our Science, that in the composition of Metals there enter two types of viscous moistures: one on the outside, which they call *extrinsic*, and the other on the inside, which they call *intrinsic*. And because the first is coarse and is not well and perfectly mixed with its earthy and subtle Matter, it is easily burned and consumed by 
<margin>8</margin> 
the fire. But the second is greatly subtle, and so mixed with its earthy part, that both together make but a single Matter; which cannot be partially consumed by the fire without being entirely consumed altogether.

->OPUSCULE<-

And from this is procreated and made the Quicksilver <term>Quicksilver: also known as mercury; "Vif-argent" in the original French literally means "living silver."</term> that we commonly see. # OF D. ZACHAIRE.

Maxims of the good and principal Authors who have preceded us. These authors use, among others, four Terms when speaking of the composition of our divine Work; namely: the **Four Elements**, the **perfect Leaven** <term>Leaven</term><note>In alchemy, a "leaven" acts like yeast in bread; it is a small amount of the perfected Stone used to "ferment" and transform a larger mass of base metal into gold.</note>, the **true Venom**, and the **perfect Coagulum** <term>Coagulum</term><note>Also called "rennet" or "curd." <margin>*Four Elements.*</margin>

# SHORT TREATISE

Decoction <term>Decoction</term><note>A process of prolonged heating or "cooking" of the substance in a sealed vessel, essential for maturing the alchemical Work.</note>, in which our Matter is fixed. This Matter—which at the beginning showed the true appearance of *Quicksilver* <term>Quicksilver</term><note>Also known as Mercury; it represents the volatile, fluid, and "feminine" principle of the Work.</note> because it was volatile—is thus, in the end, called fixed. And then that which was previously unknown within (namely the fixed parts, which we call *Sulfur* <term>Sulfur</term><note>The "masculine" principle representing heat, dry stability, and the "seed" of the metal.</note>) is made manifest by the continuous and final Decoction, in which it dominates the volatile. This is the reason why our Matter is no longer called volatile (I speak here of those who consider the final Decoction) but *fixed Sulfur*, as *Arnaldus de Villa Nova* <note>A famous 13th-century physician and alchemist; the "Rosary" mentioned is his *Rosarium Philosophorum*.</note> says in his great *Rosary*, when he spoke of the final Decoction of our divine Work. *It is*, he says, *the true red Sulfur, by which Quicksilver can be perfected into fine Gold.*

By this we can justly and truly conclude, *That the Matter from which we compose our divine Work is but one alone, entirely similar to the Matter which Nature uses underground within the mines, in the procreation of Metals*, notwithstanding the authorities we have cited above to the contrary, and all other similar ones. For as **Aristotle** says (and even experience bears witness to us) the diversity of names does not make the thing diverse.

### OPUSCULE

...son, as the same *Morien* <note>original: "Morien"; referring to Morienus Romanus, a legendary 7th-century alchemist and hermit who supposedly taught the secrets of the stone to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says; for what the <term>Theriac</term><note>A universal antidote or panacea. <margin>† *Rennet or Coagulant.*</margin>
Similar is the interpretation of the last Term, which is the most used of all, and the most misunderstood. For the majority understand it to refer to our divine Work when it is perfected. They say that just as a little <term>Rennet</term><note>original: "Caille ou Coagule"; Zachaire is using the metaphor of cheesemaking to explain how a small amount of concentrated "active" substance can solidify a large amount of liquid "passive" substance.</note> or Coagulant congeals much Milk: so a little of our Matter cast upon <term>Quicksilver</term><note>original: "Argent vif"; Mercury in its common liquid state.</note> congeals it and reduces it to its own nature. But this is to wander greatly from the truth. For they conclude by this that our Matter could not be compared to the Metals, because they are already congealed. Wherefore it must be understood that when our Mercury appears simple, it is fluid, which the Philosophers have called *Milk*, calling its *Rennet* or *Coagulant* that which we have called above *Leaven*, *Venom*, and *Theriac*. Because just as the Rennet is in no way different from the Milk except by a little <term>Decoction</term><note>original: "Decoction"; the process of boiling or heating a substance in a liquid to extract its essence or concentrate it. In alchemy, it refers to the prolonged application of heat to mature the matter.</note>; so our Coagulant is in no way different from our Mercury, except by the Decoction it has acquired beforehand. This is the great and supernatural secret which has caused and moved the Philosophers to call our Science *Divine*, because all human sense and human reasons fail therein; as we have declared before. And it is this Coagulant that *Hermes* <note>original: "Hermés"; Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of the hermetic and alchemical tradition.</note> calls *the Flower*

<summary>Denis Zachaire clarifies that alchemical terms like "Theriac," "Venom," and "Rennet" are allegories for the "Leaven" that solidifies liquid Mercury. He explains that the transformation is a natural process of "Decoction" (heating), which elevates the craft to a "Divine Science" beyond human reason.</summary>

...of Gold, which the Philosophers mean when they say that in the Congelation of the Spirit is made the true Dissolution of the Body, and conversely, in the Dissolution of the Body is made the true Congelation of the Spirit. This is because, by its means, the whole is perfected, as *Senior* <note>original: "Senior"; referring to Senior Zadith (Zadith ben Hamuel), a 10th-century Arabic alchemist whose symbolic texts were foundational to Western alchemy.</note> says. For this same reason, Alexander <note>Refers to Alexander the Great, to whom many apocryphal alchemical letters and treatises were attributed in the Middle Ages.</note> wrote that there is nothing created in our Science except that which is made of Male and Female; calling our <term>Coagulant</term><note>original: "Coagule"; the active, stabilizing agent that "curdles" or fixes the liquid Mercury into a solid state.</note> the Male because it acts—for all the Philosophers have attributed action to the Male and passion <note>In the classical sense of "passivity" or being the recipient of an action.</note> to the Female—and calling our Mercury the Female, because the said Coagulant acts and demonstrates its power upon her. 

This is the reason why they have written that the Woman has wings: because our simple Mercury is volatile; yet it is held back by the said Coagulant. This led them to write that we must make the Female ascend upon the Male, and afterwards the Male upon the Female. They mean the same thing when they say in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Tourbe des Philosophes," referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest and most famous Latin alchemical texts, written as a debate between ancient philosophers.</note>, *“That we must honor our King and the Queen his Wife, and take good care not to burn them,”* which is to say, we must not hasten our <term>Decoction</term><note>The process of "cooking" or heating the alchemical mixture over a long period. Excessive heat was believed to "burn" the delicate life-force of the metals.</note>. For as Arnaldus de Villa Nova <note>original: "Arnaud de Ville-neufve"; a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> says in his *Great Rosary*, *“The principal fault in our divine Work is the sudden decoction.”*

The ancient Philosophers wrote similar and varied Terms in their books. But because these I have mentioned are the principal ones, I will end my explanation of them; for when these are well understood, the true Matter is known; and thus all the books are explained to us and made easy, as the good *Trevisan* <note>original: "lebon Trevisan"; Bernard of Trevisan, a 15th-century alchemist famous for his long search for the Stone and his eventual "success."</note> says.

Wherefore I will conclude with all the Authors,

->*In which the Practice is shown under allegory.*<-

The Philosophers and true **Cosmographers** <term>Cosmographers</term><note>Early scholars who studied and mapped the general features of the universe, combining elements of geography, astronomy, and natural history.</note> have left in writing that the Earth, which is today habitable, is divided into three main parts; namely, Asia, Africa, and Europe, which they have said to be under four regions; the East and West, the South and North. ## How to Perform Projection Upon Metals.

To properly convert all imperfect metals <note>In alchemy, "imperfect metals" refers to lead, tin, iron, and copper, which were believed to be "sick" or "incomplete" versions of gold.</note> to the nature of our **great King** <note>The "great King" is a common name for the final, red stage of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, you must take one ounce of it, after it has been multiplied and refreshed, and cast it upon four ounces of fine melted **Gold**. You will find all your matter becomes brittle; you shall pulverize this and let it cook for three days in a proper and well-sealed **Vessel**, within the **closed mountain** <note>original: "montagne close." This is an alchemical metaphor for the sealed furnace or the "philosophical egg" (a glass flask) where the final transformation occurs.</note>, with the heat of the **final assault** <note>This refers to the highest degree of heat in the alchemical process.</note>. And of this powder, you shall cast one ounce upon twenty-five marks of **Silver**, or of **Copper**. Or else upon eighteen marks of **Lead**, or of **Tin**; Or else upon fifteen marks of common **Quicksilver** <note>original: "Argent-vif," or mercury.</note> heated in a **Crucible**, or congealed with Lead. But they must first be well melted and heated, and you will see shortly thereafter your Matter covered with a very thick foam. Then, when it has completed its operation, it will seem to you as if the **Crucible** has burst. Then you shall remelt your matter, and you will find it to be in fine **Gold**.

But if by chance you have not kept to the aforementioned weight, you will find your matters seemingly unchanged from their first color. Therefore, it will be necessary to pass them through a large **Cupel** <term>Cupel: A shallow, porous dish (often made of bone ash) used in assaying to separate precious metals from base metals, which are absorbed into the dish.</term>, without adding Lead; and within three hours after, the **Cupel** will have consumed everything that had not been perfected, for the failure of not having put in enough of our **divine Work**; and the rest will remain on top entirely pure, which you shall pass through the **Royal Cement** <term>Royal Cement: A chemical mixture (typically containing salt and brick dust) used at high heat to purify gold by removing any remaining silver or base metals.</term> for the space of six hours, and you will find all the **Gold**, which will have been converted by the help of our **great King**.

wish to follow. For I foresee that there will be many who shall be enlightened by my Book. I even know several persons who know this Secret as well as I do, and I do not doubt that there are still many other Philosophers, whose acquaintance I hope to acquire from one day to the next, and in a short time. May God do by His holy will as He pleases. I confess that I am unworthy for Him to use me to do these things. Nevertheless, in these same things, I do not cease to adore His holy will, to which all creatures must be submitted, since it is by Him alone that He created them, and it is for Him alone that He preserves them.

## CHAPTER VI.

### *The Air of the Sages.*

The extended Heaven, or the Firmament, is called **Air** in the Holy Scripture. Our **Chaos** <term>Chaos: the raw, unrefined starting material of the alchemical process, containing all elements in confusion</term> is also called Air, and in this there is a great secret. For just as the Firmamental Air is that which separates the waters; so does our Air. And consequently, our **Work** <note>original: "Oeuvre." The "Great Work" or Magnum Opus—the process of creating the Philosophers' Stone.</note> is effectively the System of the **Macrocosm** <note>original: "grand Monde." The universe at large, which the alchemist seeks to replicate in miniature.</note>. For just as we, who live upon the Earth, see the Waters that are below the Firmament; and just as they appear to us; but those which are above are out of our sight, because they are too distant from us. Likewise in our **Microcosm** <term>Microcosm: literally "little world," referring to the alchemical vessel or the human being as a reflection of the universe</term> [or little World] there are ex-central mineral Waters [that is to say, outside of their Center] which appear: But those which are enclosed within, we do not see at all, although they are indeed there. These are those Waters of which the Author of the *New Light* <note>original: "Auteur de la Nouvelle Lumiere." A reference to Michael Sendivogius (1566–1636), a famous alchemist who wrote "The New Chemical Light."</note> says there are some, but that they do not appear until it pleases the **Artist** <term>Artist: a common term for the practicing alchemist</term>. Just as the Air makes a separation between the Waters, so too our Air prevents the Waters that are outside the Center from being able to enter in any way with those that are in the Center. For if they entered, and they happened to mix together, they would immediately join in an indissoluble union.

I shall say then that the external, vaporous, burning **Sulfur** <term>Sulfur: in alchemy, one of the three primary principles, representing the active, masculine, and combustible nature of matter</term> is stubbornly attached to our Chaos, whose tyranny unable...

You have need here that **Diana** be favorable to you, she who knows how to tame wild beasts, who has two **Doves** that will temper with their wings the malignity of the Air, because the Young Man enters easily through the pores; he first shakes the cataracts and the reservoirs that are in the air, and opens them, and he forms a displeasing cloud. Then make the Waters come over the top, until the whiteness of the Moon appears. Thus by the command of God, the Light will appear. Separate seven times the Light from the Darkness, and our philosophical creation of **Mercury** will be accomplished. And the seventh day will be for you a **Sabbath** <term>Sabbath: the final stage of rest or fixation in the alchemical process, where the matter is no longer volatile and has reached a state of stable perfection.</term> of rest. So that from that time on, until a year later it is completed—

The goal is to reach the "white" stage of Diana, where the substance is cleansed of its "leprosy" and becomes a stable, purified base.</summary>

## CHAPTER VII.

### Concerning the first Operation of the preparation of the Philosophical Mercury, by the flying Eagles.

You must know, my Brother, that the exact preparation of the **Eagles** <term>Eagles: A symbolic term for the process of sublimation—the vaporization and re-solidification of a substance—or for the volatile metallic spirits used to dissolve gold.</term> of the Philosophers is considered the first degree of perfection; and that to know it, one must be skillful and have a good Mind. For do not imagine that any of Us reached this **Science** <note>original: "Science." Here meaning the "Sacred Art" or Alchemy itself.</note> by chance, or by a fortuitous imagination, as the ignorant commoner foolishly believes. We have worked much and for a long time; we have spent many nights without sleep, and we have taken great pains to discover the truth. You, therefore, who desire to reach this Science, be strongly persuaded that if you do not work, and if you do not take pains, you will never achieve anything. I mean this in the **first Operation**. For in the second, it is **Nature** alone who does all the Work, without any need to put a hand to it, except only to maintain a moderate fire on the outside. Understand well then, my Brother, what the Philosophers mean when they say that one must lead their **Eagles** to devour the **Lion** <term>Lion: Often represents "Green Lion" (raw ore or mineral) or "Red Lion" (fixed gold). To "devour" the lion means to dissolve the solid metal into a liquid, mercurial state.</term>; and that the fewer Eagles there are, the more rugged the combat is,

<sig>X iiij</sig>

<summary>Philalethes introduces the "flying Eagles" (sublimations) as the essential first step in preparing the Philosophical Mercury, emphasizing the hard work required of the alchemist. He contrasts the labor-intensive first stage with the second stage, where Nature completes the work autonomously under a gentle heat.</summary>

From this will be made the **Chameleon**, or our **Chaos**, in which are hidden all...

### CHAPTER VIII.

->*Of the tedious labor of the first preparation.*<-

Some ignorant people, namely the chemists <note>The author uses "chemists" (Chymistes) here as a term of derision for "puffers"—those who practice chemistry purely as a mechanical or commercial craft without understanding the deeper "Philosophical" secrets.</note>, have wished to imagine that our entire Work, from the beginning until the end, is but a recreation full of amusement, and that it is in no way laborious. But let them feed, if they so choose, upon their own imagination. It is certain that in a work which they persuade themselves to be so easy, they will gather nothing but wind from their vain imagination and their idle operations. As for us, we are certain that, after the Blessing of God and a good root <note>The "root" refers to the starting matter or the fundamental substance of the Work.</note>, it is labor, industry, and care that constitute the main part of our business. And certainly, the labor employed in the bustle of the household—which should rather pass for a game and a diversion than for a hardship—cannot give us the satisfaction that we so passionately desire. On the contrary, one must not, as Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of the alchemical tradition.</note> says, pretend to spare one’s effort, even if it should trouble one's health. For otherwise, what the Sage <note>The "Sage" refers to King Solomon; the author is quoting Proverbs 21:25.</note> predicted in his Proverbs will be found true: namely, that the desire of the lazy man shall kill him. And it is no wonder if so many people who work at Alchemy become poor, because they do not love labor and do not wish to spend <note>The original "faire de dépense" implies both the expenditure of money and the expenditure of effort/energy.</note>. ## CHAPTER IX.

### *On the power of our Mercury over all other Metals.*

Our Mercury is the Serpent that devoured the companions of Cadmus <note>In Greek mythology, Cadmus slew a dragon/serpent; in alchemy, this myth describes the interaction between the "metallic seed" (Cadmus) and the "solvent" (the Serpent/Mercury).</note>, and it is not to be wondered at, since it had already devoured Cadmus himself, who was much stronger than they. Philalethes famously describes the necessity of seven to nine "flights of the Eagle" to perfect the Mercury.</note>, or of two, or at most three, commands <term>Saturn</term> <note>The metal Lead.</note>, <term>Jupiter</term> <note>The metal Tin.</note>, and <term>Venus</term> <note>The metal Copper.</note>. It commands the <term>Moon</term> <note>The metal Silver.</note> from three Eagles up to seven; and finally, when it has up to ten Eagles, it commands the <term>Sun</term> <note>The metal Gold.</note>. Therefore, I declare that this Mercury is closer to the <term>First Being</term> <note>The *Prima Materia*, or the original, undifferentiated substance from which all metals grow in the earth.</note> (or matter) of metals than any other Mercury. It is for this reason that it radically penetrates metallic bodies, and makes manifest and creates...

## CHAPTER XI.

### *How the perfect Magistery was found.*

All the Sages who in former times acquired the knowledge of this <term>Art</term> <note>Alchemy was traditionally called "the Art" or "the Royal Art" by its practitioners.</note>, without any book, were moved by the inspiration of God to seek and acquire it in the manner I am about to describe. For I cannot believe that anyone has ever possessed it immediately by revelation—unless, perhaps, one wishes to say that Solomon knew it, which I prefer to leave undecided rather than meddling in an attempt to decide it. But even if it were true that he knew it, can one conclude from this that he did not acquire it through research and study? For he asked God only for Wisdom, which He gave him in such a way that he possessed along with it both riches and peace. Since, therefore, he carefully studied and examined the nature of Plants and Trees, from the Cedar that is in Lebanon to the Hyssop on the walls <note>This is a reference to 1 Kings 4:33, describing King Solomon's vast knowledge of the natural world.</note>; who would be a man of good sense who could deny that he also applied himself to the knowledge of the nature of <term>Minerals</term>, which is no less agreeable than the other?

But let us resume our discourse. ### C H A P T E R XII.

->*The general manner of performing the perfect Magistery.*<- <term>Magistery</term> <note>From the Latin "Magisterium"; the master process or the successful completion of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>

We must forever give thanks to God that it has pleased Him to show us these secrets of Nature, which He has hidden from the eyes of many. This is what obliges us to freely and faithfully reveal to those who, like us, are lovers of this science, that which we have freely received from the liberality of this great Benefactor. Know then that the greatest secret of our **Operation** <note>The alchemical process of transformation.</note> is nothing other than a **cohobation** <term>Cohobation</term> <note>The repeated process of pouring a distilled liquid back onto the solid matter from which it was drawn to intensify its properties.</note> of the natures one upon the other, until the perfectly digested and cooked virtue is extracted from the digested matter by means of the raw material.

<margin>></margin>And for this purpose, one must first have, prepare, and accurately arrange all the things that enter into the **Work** <term>Work</term> <note>The "Great Work" (Magnum Opus), the ultimate goal of the alchemist.</note>.
<margin>></margin>Secondly, one must well arrange the external conditions.
<margin>></margin>Thirdly, the things being thus ready and prepared, one requires a good **Regimen** <term>Regimen</term> <note>The controlled management of fire and stages of the process.</note>.
<margin>></margin>Fourthly, before beginning to work, one must have knowledge and understand everything that appears in the Work, so as not to work blindly.
<margin>></margin>Fifthly and finally, one must have patience, so that the Work is not hurried, nor governed and pushed with haste. We shall speak of all these things in order, one after the other; and we shall say as much about them as a brother can say to his brother.

## CHAPTER XIII.

### On the Use of Ripe Sulfur in the Work of the Elixir.

We have spoken of the necessity of **Mercury** <term>Mercury</term> <note>In alchemy, Mercury represents the fluid, passive, and feminine principle of matter, often called the "Spirit."</note>, and we have revealed many secrets concerning Mercury which, before our time, were quite rare and unknown in the world. This is because almost all books of **Chemistry** <note>The author uses "Chemistry" here in the sense of "Alchemy," the quest for the Philosopher's Stone.</note> are full of nothing but enigmas, or **sophistical operations** <note>False or deceptive processes that do not lead to the true Stone.</note>, or finally, a heap and a confusion of superfluous words <gloss>a</gloss>. For my part, I have not acted in this manner, submitting a true will to the good pleasure of God, who it seems to me intends to open and reveal these treasures in this **last age of the world** <note>Many 17th-century alchemists believed they were living in an era of divine revelation before the end of time.</note>.

Thus, I no longer fear that this Art will become vile and contemptible. I wish for that not to happen, and indeed it cannot, because true **Wisdom** <note>Often used as a synonym for the knowledge of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> preserves itself and maintains itself in eternal honor. But would to God that Gold and Silver—those two great Idols which have until now been adored by the whole world—might become as contemptible as mud and manure. For I, who know the Art of making them, would not be in such pain to hide who I am. It seems that the **curse of Cain** <note>According to the Bible, Cain was condemned to be a "restless wanderer." Philalethes feels that his secret knowledge forces him into a life of perpetual travel and anonymity to escape those who would exploit him.</note> has fallen upon me (a thought I cannot have without shedding tears and sighing), and that I am, like him, driven out—

But if you make friends with prudent persons, you must be well-advised, and take great care that others cannot recognize you as easily as you believe you can discover a Philosopher, and draw his **Secret** <term>The "Secret" refers to the knowledge of the Philosopher's Stone and the transmutation of metals.</term> from him, provided only that you had his conversation. Even then, you would have great difficulty perceiving that he had this suspicion of you, without receiving much inconvenience from it. Furthermore, it is enough for someone to have the slightest conjecture in the world about your **Secret** for ambushes to be set for you. Men are so wicked that I know some have been hanged on this simple suspicion, who nevertheless knew nothing. It only required that some desperate people had merely heard mention of this **Science** <note>original: "Science" — in alchemical texts, this refers to the "Sacred Art" or the "Hermetic Science" of alchemy.</note> and that those they suspected had the reputation of knowing it.

I would be too long-winded and too tedious if I wished to recount all that I have experienced, seen, and heard said regarding this affair—and more so in this present time than in any other of the past centuries. And truly, do we not see that **Alchemy** is a pretext that everyone uses; so that if

If you do the slightest thing in secret, you will hardly be able to take three steps before you are betrayed. The precautions you take to hide yourself will only incite the curiosity of those who wish to observe you more closely; they will spread rumors that you are making **counterfeit money**. In short, what will they not say? 

But if you choose to act more openly: since the things you do will be surprising and extraordinary, whether in **Medicine** or in **Chemistry** <term>Chymie: In the 17th century, this term covered both spiritual alchemy and practical chemical experiments.</term>; if you have some large ingot of **Fine Gold** or **Pure Silver** that you wish to sell, people will be astonished to see such a great quantity of gold so fine and silver so pure. They will be at a loss to know where it could come from, especially since gold of such fineness comes from nowhere; unless perhaps from **Barbary** <note>The "Barbary Coast" was a term used by Europeans for the North African coastal regions.</note> or **Guinea**, from which very fine gold is brought in tiny grains like sand. <margin>a This gold is fished from the River Niger.</margin> *a* And the gold that you possess, being of an even higher **Carat** and in the form of an ingot, will give great cause for murmuring. 

Merchants are not so foolish, though they may say, like children at play, "Our eyes are closed, come, we see nothing": if you are gullible enough to go to them, in a single blink of an eye they will discover more than enough to cause you much harm and trouble. As for fine **Silver**, none comes from any place that is as pure as that which we make through our **Art** <note>In this context, "Art" refers to the Great Work of Alchemical transmutation.</note>. Very good silver is brought from **Spain**, which is nevertheless hardly better than the **Sterling Silver** of **England**, and even then its coinage is much more poorly made; furthermore, it can only be transported in secret, because it is forbidden by the laws of the country. If you go, then, to sell a large quantity of fine silver, you will reveal yourself by that act, and if you wish to alloy it—not being a Goldsmith or a Minter—you deserve death by the laws...

our only **Mercury** <term>Mercury: Not common quicksilver, but the "solvent" of the philosophers used to dissolve metals.</term>, and it is from this Mercury that it receives the multiplication of its seed, not so much in weight, as in virtue <note>In alchemy, "virtue" refers to the inherent power, potency, or medicinal strength of a substance.</note>. And it would always remain in that state (neither germinating nor producing) if it were always kept in a dry place and in dry air. But if one sows it, and throws it into the earth, this grain immediately receives fermentative life <note>A term used to describe the biological "triggering" of growth, which alchemists believed was mirrored in the chemical world.</note>; it swells, it softens, and it germinates. 

This is precisely what happens in our Gold; it is dead, which is to say that its vivifying virtue is sealed and locked away under its corporeal bark <note>The "corporeal bark" or crust refers to the hard, metallic exterior of the gold that prevents its internal "spirit" from acting.</note>, just as it is in a grain of Wheat; though differently. For there is a great difference between a grain, which is vegetable, and Gold, which is a Metal. But Gold, just like the grain of wheat, remains always without being changed if it is held in dry air: and it is destroyed in the fire, and can only be reduced (into its seed) in our **Water** <term>Water: The philosophical solvent, often synonymous with Mercury, capable of dissolving metals back to their first matter.</term> alone; and then our grain is living.

And just as Wheat, when sown in the field, changes its name and is called the "Farmer's Seed," which, while it was in the granary, was only Wheat, and was as suited for making bread or some other similar thing as it was for being Seed. Thus Gold, while it is in the form of a ring, or a vase, or a piece of Coin, is then Vulgar Gold.

# CHAPTER XVIII.

## Of the Furnace or the Athanor <term>Athanor: A furnace used by alchemists designed to maintain a uniform and constant heat over long periods of time, often called a "tower furnace."</term> of the Philosophers.

I have spoken enough of **Mercury**, of its preparation, of its proportion, and of its virtue. I have also sufficiently discoursed on **Sulphur**, of its necessity and of its use in our **Work**. I have advised how it was necessary to prepare them; I have shown how it was necessary to mix them; and I have declared many things regarding the **vessel**, in which they must be placed and sealed. But I give warning that all I have said must be understood with a grain of salt <note>original: "grain de sel." This is an explicit instruction to the reader to look for metaphorical or hidden meanings.</note>, [and with prudence and discretion,] for fear that if one intended to take things literally, and proceed word for word as I have said, one would often make mistakes. For I have so intermingled the subtleties of **Philosophy** with a most extraordinary ingenuity, that if one does not help oneself by explaining and understanding metaphorically several things I have said in the preceding Chapters; one will gather no other fruit than loss and useless expense. For example, when I said that without any ambiguity one of the principles or materials was **Mercury**, and the other was the **Sun** <note>original: "Soleil." In alchemy, the Sun represents Gold.</note>: that one was sold, and the other had to be made by **Art** <term>Art: referring specifically to the Alchemical Art or the Great Work.</term>; You must know that our **Mercury** gives **Gold** from itself, and you do not know that it is the subject of our **Secrets**. You have only to sell it for the common **Sun**, being true **Sun** by every kind of test.

# CHAPTER XXI.

## *On the Combustion of the Flowers, & how it can be prevented.*

It is a mistake of no small consequence, and one which nonetheless occurs easily—the combustion or burning of the flowers <note>In alchemy, "flowers" (original: *fleurs*) refers to the volatile spirits or substances that rise and sublimate at the top of the vessel.</note> before the Natures, still tender, are properly extracted from their depth and their center. One must principally take care not to make this mistake after the third week. For in the beginning there is such a great abundance of moisture <term>humeur: the liquid or vaporous component of the alchemical mixture</term>, that if you apply a fire stronger than necessary, your vessel (which is fragile) will not be able to resist the quantity of winds <note>Gases or vapors produced during heating.</note> that will form within it, which will immediately cause it to burst, unless the vessel is larger than required. And if this should happen, the humidity will be so dispersed and scattered that it will no longer return to its Body <note>The solid matter remaining at the bottom of the vessel.</note>, at least not in such a quantity as to be sufficient to give it strength and vigor. 

But when the Earth <note>The dry, solid residue.</note> has begun to retain a part of its Water, and vapors are no longer forming, one may indeed increase the fire more than necessary without fear that the vessel might be damaged in any way. Yet this will also cause the Work to be spoiled, and it will take on the color of the wild poppy <note>original: "pavot sauvage." A bright red color; in this context, it signifies a premature and failed "reddening" of the matter.</note>, and the entire composition will finally become a dry Powder, which will have turned Red uselessly. This sign will let you know that the Fire was stronger than it should have been; that is to say, so strong that it will have

<summary>Philalethes warns the alchemist against using excessive heat in the early weeks of the process, which can cause the vessel to explode or result in a useless, prematurely red powder. He explains that moisture must be carefully managed so it can eventually return to the solid "body" of the matter.</summary>

## CHAPTER XXII.

### *The Regimen of Saturn: What it is and why it is so called.*

All the Philosophers who have written of this labor have spoken of the Work and the regimen of Saturn <note>In alchemy, Saturn is the traditional name for the planet associated with the metal Lead. It also represents the "Nigredo" or black stage—the first phase of the Great Work, characterized by decomposition and the "death" of the initial ingredients.</note>, which has been the cause why several, not understanding them well, have fallen into many errors and been deceived in their opinion. There are some who, because of this, have worked upon common Lead with more hope than profit.

But know that our Lead <note>Alchemists frequently distinguished between "vulgar" (common) metals and "philosophical" metals—the latter being the special, purified substances prepared through their secret processes.</note> is more precious than any Gold whatsoever. For it is the mud and the slime in which the soul of Gold joins with Mercury, in order to then produce the Male and the Female <note>These terms refer to the two primary principles of alchemy: Sulphur (the active, masculine principle) and Mercury (the passive, feminine principle), whose union produces the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, just as God created Adam and Eve his wife from the slime of the earth.

Therefore, as He who was the highest and most exalted humbled himself here to be made the lowest, it must be hoped that in his blood the Redemption of all the Brothers shall be accomplished <note>This is a common alchemical metaphor where the transformation of the stone mirrors the Passion and Resurrection of Christ; the "Redemption of the Brothers" refers to the transmutation of "base" metals into "noble" ones.</note>. Thus, what we call Saturn in our Work is the tomb where our King is buried, and it is the key to the treasure of the Art. Happy is he who can see this Planet which moves so slowly. Pray to God, my Brother, that He may grant you this grace; for it is a blessing that depends not on him who runs to have it, nor on him who desires it, but on the Father of lights alone <note>original: "Pere des lumieres," a biblical reference to James 1:17. Alchemists believed that the final secret of the Stone was a "Donum Dei" (Gift of God) granted only to the virtuous.</note>.

### CHAPTER XXIII.

#### *Of the Different Regimens of this Work.*

All those who study our Science must be fully persuaded that in the entire Work of the Stone, it is only the Regimen <note>The "regimen" refers to the specific management of heat, timing, and the internal environment of the alchemical vessel. It is often considered the most difficult part of the process to master.</note> alone that has been hidden from them. And what a Philosopher has said of it is very true: *whoever has perfect knowledge of it will be honored by Princes and the great ones of the earth.* And I swear to you on my faith that if the Regimen were only described openly (and as it must be performed), there is not even a Fool who would not mock our Art. For to one who once knows it, *all the rest is but women’s work and children’s play* <note>The phrase "women's work and children's play" (Latin: *opus mulierum et ludus puerorum*) is a traditional alchemical expression. It implies that once the secret of the heat is understood, the process becomes simple, requiring only patience and steady cooking.</note>, there being nothing else left to do but to Cook. And this is what has obliged the Philosophers to hide this secret with great artifice; and believe surely that I have fundamentally done the same thing. Nevertheless, since I said I would act sincerely and in good faith in this small Treatise, and since I have promised it, I find myself obliged to do something special, so as not to deceive the hope and the labor of the people of spirit who read this Book.

Know then that in all our Work we have only a single *linear* Regimen <note>A "linear" regimen suggests a single, continuous process of heating and maturation without changing the vessel or the fundamental approach, even as the matter evolves through different colors.</note>, which is nothing other than to cook and to digest. And nevertheless, this single Regimen includes several others within itself, which the envious <note>In alchemy, "envious" authors were those who deliberately obscured their recipes with metaphors and riddles to prevent the "unworthy" from discovering the secret.</note> have hidden by giving them many different names, and have spoken of them as if they were different Operations. For my part, because I promised
