## CHAPTER XXIV.

### Of the First Regimen of the Work, Which is that of Mercury.

I shall begin with the Regimen of Mercury, which is a secret of which not one of the Philosophers has ever spoken. For they have all begun with the second work, that is to say, with the Regimen of Saturn, and they have given no light regarding what occurs before the blackness <term>nigredo: the first major stage of the Great Work, symbolizing the death or decomposition of the matter, represented by the color black</term> appears—which is one of the principal signs of the Work. Even the good Trevisan <note>Bernard Trevisan (1406–1490) was a legendary alchemist. His "Parable" is a famous allegorical story describing the chemical process through the metaphor of a King bathing in a fountain.</note> said nothing of it. For he says in his Parable that when the King comes to the Fountain, having left all foreign persons behind, he enters the Bath all alone, wearing a robe of cloth-of-gold, which he strips off and gives to Saturn, who in return gives him a doublet of black velvet. But he does not say at all how long it takes for the King to remove and strip off this cloth-of-gold robe, and thus he passes over in silence an entire Regimen, which lasts perhaps forty days, and sometimes fifty. ### CHAPTER XXV.

->Of the second Regimen of the Work, which is that of Saturn.<-

THE Regimen of Mercury being finished, (which one recognizes because its Operation is to strip the King of his robes of cloth of Gold, and to attack and weary him by various combats of the Lion until he is at his last gasp) the Regimen of Saturn succeeds him. For it is the will of God that the Work which is begun should be completed in the manner it ought to be, and it is the Rule of this tragedy that when one of the characters exits the Stage, the other enters at the same time; once one has played his role, the other begins his immediately after. Thus the Regimen of Mercury is no sooner finished than Saturn—who is his successor and to whom the Kingdom belongs by right of succession—takes his place immediately. The Lion being dead, the Raven <note>The "Raven" or "Crow" is the traditional alchemical symbol for the *nigredo* stage, where the matter undergoes putrefaction and turns black.</note> comes to be born. And this Regimen is very straightforward and linear regarding the heat, because there is only one single and unique color that appears, which is the blackest black; but there are neither fumes, nor wind, nor any symbol (or sign) of life, and one notices nothing else except that the Composition sometimes appears completely dry, and at times one sees that it boils in the manner (and consistency) of molten pitch. Oh, what a frightful thing to see! Truly, it is a proper representation of eternal death, yet it is something that should cause joy to the Artist <term>Artist: the alchemist or practitioner of the Hermetic art.</term>! # CHAPTER XXVII.

->Of the Regimen of the Moon.<-

The Regimen of Jupiter being completed, toward the end of the fourth month the sign of the Crescent of the Moon will appear to you, and you should know that the entire Regimen of Jupiter was employed in washing the **Laton** <note>Laton (or Latten) refers to the base, "unclean" metallic matter that must be purified through washing and whitening to reach the state of silver.</note>. The **Spirit** that performs this *lotion* [or which washes it] is very white in its Nature, but the **Body** that must be washed is of a most deep Black. And before it has passed from this blackness to whiteness, all the colors that exist between black and white will have appeared; once these have finished, everything becomes white—though it is not yet perfectly white from the very first day. For from white it will only reach perfect whiteness little by little, and by degrees. And you should know that in this **Regimen**, the **Matter** appears to the sight as if it were entirely like flowing **Quicksilver** <term>Argent-vif: The traditional term for mercury, meaning "living silver," representing the fluid, transformative state of the matter.</term>. And this is what is called sealing the **Mother** in the womb of her **Child** whom she previously brought forth. And in this **Regimen**, many beautiful **Colors** will be seen, which will only show themselves and disappear immediately, but which will nevertheless lean more toward whiteness than Blackness; just as in the **Regimen of Jupiter**, they approached blackness more than whiteness.

->*Of the Regimen of Venus.*<-

It is the most surprising and admirable thing of all regarding our **Stone** that, being now entirely perfect and able—in the state it is in—to communicate a perfect **Tincture** <term>Tincture: A potent medicinal or transmutative essence. ### PHILALETHES.

Nevertheless, if you thought to take it out of its **Vessel** <term>Vessel: The glass flask, often called a "philosopher's egg," used to contain the matter during the Work.</term>, to put it into another once it has cooled, you would no longer be able to push it to a higher degree of perfection, no matter what skill you might employ. And neither I nor any of the ancient Philosophers could give a convincing reason why this is so; we can say nothing else, except that it is the good pleasure of God that it happens in this way.

Here you must take great care to manage your **fire** well. For it is an indubitable maxim that the **Stone**, to be perfect, must be **Fusible** <term>Fusible: Capable of being melted. In alchemy, the Stone must flow like wax rather than shatter like stone or turn into unworkable glass.</term>. And this is that vitrification of the Matter that the Philosophers so often warn must be avoided, and which (if one is not very careful) is accustomed to happening before the **Work** is at the **perfect white** <note>The "perfect white" refers to the Albedo stage, the second major milestone of the Great Work, signifying purity and the creation of the White Stone.</note>, and even when it is there. And this occurs from the middle of the **Regimen of the Moon**, until the seventh or tenth day of that of **Venus**. You must therefore increase the fire only a little; and in such a way that the heat cannot make the **Composition** flow like glass. Instead, the heat must be gentle, because by this means the Matter will melt and swell of its own accord, and with the help of God, it will receive a **Spirit** that will take flight and rise upward, and will carry and lift the Stone with itself, and it will produce and bring forth new **Colors**. The first of all will be the **greenness of Venus** <note>In the alchemical sequence, green often represents the "Green Lion" or the beginning of a new life/growth phase after the purity of the white stage.</note>, which will last a long time; for it will not entirely disappear until after twenty days.

## *Of the Regimen of the Sun.*

# CHAPTER XXXII.

## *The Imbibition of the Stone.*

I know well that there are many Authors who, in this Work, take Fermentation to be the internal and invisible Agent, because they call "Ferment" that which has the power to thicken the volatile and subtle Spirits without any need to touch them for that purpose. But I, who am not accustomed to citing others, nor to subjecting myself to their opinions in a matter that I know as well as they, have spoken of it according to the knowledge and experience I have of it.

### CHAPTER XXXIII.

->The Multiplication of the Stone.<-

THERE is no other way to perform the Multiplication than to take the Stone when it is perfect, and put one part of it with three, or at most with four parts of Mercury of the first Operation (that is to say, the Mercury of the Philosophers <note>Philosophical Mercury is not common quicksilver, but a specialized solvent prepared through earlier alchemical stages.</note>) and give to this Composition a suitable fire for seven days, having beforehand sealed your Vessel very exactly. And you will have a very great pleasure in seeing that it will pass through all the Regimes <note>The "Regimes" are the successive stages of the alchemical process, traditionally associated with different colors and planetary rulers (e.g., the Regime of Saturn/Blackness, the Regime of Jupiter/Gray, etc.).</note> right away. And the whole will be increased in virtue <note>In this context, "virtue" refers to the inherent power, potency, or strength of the alchemical medicine.</note> a thousand times more than the Stone was before this Multiplication. If you do the same thing a second time, it will pass through all the Regimes in three days, and its Tinging virtue will increase again by a thousand times as much. And you will make your Work pass through all the Regimes, and through all the Colors in the space of one natural day, if you reiterate the same operation for a third time. And finally, all this will be done in one hour if, for the fourth time, you do the same thing; so that you can never find the end of the virtue of your Stone, which will be so great that it will be infinite, and consequently incomprehensible, if you continue to multiply it. Having reached that point, do not forget to give immortal thanks to God; for you have in your possession the entire treasure of Nature.

## CHAPTER XXXIV.

### The Manner of Performing the Projection.

Take of your Stone when it is perfected in the manner that has been described, whether it be in the white or in the red; and according to the quality (and the degree) of your Medicine <note>The "Medicine" is a common alchemical term for the Philosopher's Stone, emphasizing its power to "heal" or perfect base metals.</note>, take four parts of one or the other luminary (that is to say, either of the Moon or of the Sun) <note>In alchemical symbolism, the "Sun" refers to gold and the "Moon" to silver.</note>. Melt them in a very clean crucible, and then throw in your white or red stone, according to whether the Luminary you have melted is white or red. And when everything is mixed and incorporated, turn over the crucible, and you will find a mass that can be pulverized.

Take one part of the powder of this composition, and ten parts of well-washed Mercury: Heat them until the Mercury begins to crackle and quiver <note>original: "petiller & de fremir." This describes the physical reaction of quicksilver just before it begins to boil or vaporize.</note>; then throw your powder onto this Mercury, and it will penetrate it in the blink of an eye. Melt all of this by increasing the fire, and the whole will be converted into a Medicine of the lower Order. 

Then take one part of this Medicine, and perform the projection upon as much of any metal as your Stone is able to tinge <note>To "tinge" or "tincture" means to fundamentally change the color and nature of the metal.</note>—when it is in fusion and has been purged—and you will have a Gold or a Silver better than any natural Gold or Silver. It is, however, better to perform the Projection little by little, until you see that your Stone can no longer tinge any more imperfect metal. For in this manner it will extend itself, and it will tinge more, because when one projects only a little of the powder upon much...

## CHAPTER XXXV.

### *Of the various uses of the Stone.*

I do not see what a man—who by the blessing of God has once perfectly accomplished this Work—would have to wish for in this world after that, except that he might, in all liberty and without fearing the deceptions and malices of the wicked, serve and honor his God all his life. For it would be an altogether unbearable vanity if a person to whom God had granted so great a grace had the ambition to appear with pomp and brilliance in the world to make themselves admired. No, believe me, those who possess this Science <note>The "Science" refers to the "Great Work" of alchemy.</note> are very far from having such thoughts; on the contrary, there is nothing they despise more.

But here is the happiness and the felicity of him to whom God has deigned to give this *Talent* <note>A likely reference to the biblical Parable of the Talents, suggesting that alchemical knowledge is a divine gift to be managed wisely.</note>. First, if he were to live a thousand years, and had every day a thousand thousand men to feed and maintain, he would never lack for anything for that purpose, knowing the manner of multiplying his Stone in weight and in virtue <note>In alchemy, "virtue" refers to the inherent power, potency, or "strength" of the substance.</note>. So that he could *transmute* into Gold or into Sil-

### *on the Translation of*
## *Philalethes.*

<image-desc>A large decorative drop-cap "I" featuring floral ornaments.</image-desc>

I Have produced the Translation of this Treatise based on the Copy that was printed in *Amsterdam* in the year 1667, which followed the Edition that *Mr. Langius* <note>Joachim Lange (1629–1694), a German physician who published several important alchemical works.</note> had commissioned in *Hamburg* a year earlier—this being the first edition to appear. And although he produced it (as he states in his *Preface*) from a single manuscript copy that was not very accurate, I would have wished to have been able to obtain a copy [of that Hamburg edition], because there must undoubtedly be fewer errors in it than in the one from *Holland*. I have endeavored to correct the most significant of these errors in this Translation, while nevertheless always adhering to the meaning and intention of the Author, as far as I have been able to discern it, as will be seen through these *Remarks*.

It was three years ago that I made this Translation at the request of a very curious person of quality <note>In the 17th century, a "person of quality" referred to someone of noble or high social standing; "curious" implied they were a seeker of knowledge or a collector of rare information.</note>, who does not understand *Latin* <note>original: "Latin". This confirms the original text translated into French was the Latin work *Introitus apertus ad occlusum regis palatium* (Open Entrance to the Closed Palace of the King).</note>, without having had the intention of having it printed. This is what obliged me, in order to make it easier for them, to frequently add several words to the Text, either to explain what preceded in a more intelligible manner, or to complete the meaning, which in some places appeared imperfect. And as this Version, being printed, must not

# REMARKS.

...only serve those who cannot understand the Latin original, I have left those additions which I believed could be useful to them; which I have taken care to distinguish from the words of the Author, enclosing them between two marks in this manner [ ] although sometimes instead of these marks, the Printer has used those of parentheses.

->For the Title, I have taken the name of **PHILALETHES** <note>Eirenaeus Philalethes was the pseudonym of a famous 17th-century alchemist, now widely believed to be the American-born George Starkey.</note> which the Author gave himself, because it is shorter than the *Open Entrance to the Closed Palace of the King* <note>original: "Entrée Ouverte du Palais fermé du Roy"; the full Latin title is *Introitus apertus ad occlusum regis palatium*.</note>.<-

Here are the principal places that I either did not understand well, or that I found faulty in the Latin Copy.

In Chapter III, there is in the Latin Copy on page 6, as noted at the bottom of page 243 of this Book: *The wise saw it in the Age of the Magi, and were stunned* <note>original: "Viderunt sapientes in Evo Magi, & obstupuerunt."</note>. I confess that I do not know what this word *Evo* written with a simple capital E means. For I do not recognize it as a Technical Term <term>Term of the Art: a specialized vocabulary word used specifically within alchemical practice.</term>, and I do not believe it to be important; thus, I have not translated it. If it were *in their age* <note>original: "in ævo suo"</note>, that would mean the Sages had seen it in their own times. But in that, there would be nothing particular, nor anything that could provide any light for the Science <note>The "Science" refers to the "Great Work" or "Hermetic Science"—the study of alchemy.</note>. It seems likely, if there is no error in this place, that the Author took it for the Region of the East, because of the name of the Magi <note>The Magi, or "Wise Men," were associated with the East in both biblical and esoteric traditions.</note> which follows, and which I have not translated, to distance myself from the Allegory he seems to want to make here with one of the Mysteries of our Religion; because that is useless and serves nothing for the understanding of the Art.

In Chapter VI: *May Diana be favorable to you here, she who knows how to tame wild beasts, whose two doves...* <note>original: "Esto hic tibi Diana propitia quæ feras domare novit, cujus bina Columba". In alchemy, Diana often symbolizes moon-governed substances or silver, while her doves typically represent the volatile spirits or white fumes produced during heating.</note>

In Chap. XI. page 257. *But that these things having been corrupted by accident, this Production which was not mature, fell of its own accord.* that is to say, *It could not become Metal because of the poor conditions of the place where it is found.* What follows immediately after is confused. It reads *thus it is seen as a certain thing deprived of movement and life* <note>original: "sic quod privatum quoddam motu vitaque conspicitur."</note>. page 20. of the Latin Edition. I could have translated it: *Thus it appears a thing deprived of some movement & of life, or deprived in some fashion.* But I have translated it as if the Latin read *and thus [Mercury] is seen as deprived in some way of movement and life* <note>original: "sicque privatus (Mercurius) quodammodo motu vitaque conspicitur."</note>. Because this reading seemed more natural to me; & to have more connection with what precedes and what follows.

In the same Chap. page 20. of the Latin *Finally they took the Offspring of Saturn into their hands* <note>original: "Tandem Saturni Sobolem in manus sumpserunt."</note>. I have translated it page 258. *Finally they tried it on the Child of Saturn.* Not wanting to put *the son of Saturn*, which would mean Jupiter <note>In mythology, Jupiter is the son of Saturn; in alchemy, the translator avoids "Son" to prevent confusion with other planetary/metallic symbols.</note>, I used instead the term *Child* which is more general. I had wanted to put *Offspring of Saturn*, as I later put *Race of Saturn*; but this word, although just as meaningful, seemed less intelligible to me than the word *Child*.

# REMARKS.

<header>->REMARKS.<-</header>

Then on the same page of the Latin: *And they proved that Stylange of gold* <note>original: "Illamque probaverunt auri Stylangen"</note>. I do not know what this word *Stylange* means, as it is neither a term of the Art <term>Term of the Art: Technical jargon used specifically by alchemists to describe their processes or materials.</term>, to my knowledge, nor is it Latin or Greek. I have translated it as *the Testing of Gold*, because I found that this expression produced a tolerable meaning. Perhaps *stylange* is a German word or from another foreign language that I do not know, which the Author has Latinized.

In the same Chapter, page 259: *Nevertheless, the little that remained did not fail to prevent this Sulfur from being able to enter in any way*. The Latin reads: *yet it prevented all entry* <note>original: "tamen omnem prohiberet ingressum"</note>. I could have translated this as *prevented this Sulfur from being entering and penetrating, or penetrative*, which are terms of the Art; but I believed that the first explanation was just as intelligible.

In the same Chapter, page 260: *But having been made volatile, until in its distillation it left no dregs* <note>The translator uses "fœces," a Latin term for the dregs or sediment remaining after a chemical process.</note>. They neglected to include these words *in its distillation*.

In the Latin on page 22, it reads: *But having also been made volatile, it would leave nothing* <note>original: "At volatilis factus quoque nullam relinqueret"</note>, etc., where there is no sense to be made, whether one places the comma after *also* <note>Latin: "quoque"</note>, or leaves it before. I have translated it as if the word were *until* <note>Latin: "quousque"</note>, and have joined what follows, which is separated by a period in the Latin.

In Chapter XIII, page 25 of the Latin: *However much he bore the face of an honest man and showed public affairs* <note>original: "Vt ut honesti faciem gesserit Resque publicas ostenderit"</note>. I have translated it: *I have seen almost no one, whatever appearance of an honest man he had, and however devoted he appeared for the public good*, etc., page 263, being unable to give another meaning to this word *showed* <note>Latin: "ostenderit"</note>, which is surely corrupted. It is true that in this place it does not con- <note>The text breaks off here; the catchword "s'a-" suggests the next page begins with "s'agit," meaning "it concerns" or "it is about."</note>

In the same Chapter 13, page 30 of the Latin: *But just as a grain remains forever unchanged in dry air, is destroyed in fire, is reducible in our water, and then is our grain* <note>original: "Verùm quemadmodum granum in aëre sicco in perpetuum impermutatum manet, in igne destruitur, in aqua nostra est reducibile, & tunc est granum nostrum."</note>. It is certain that after the adverb *But* <note>Latin: "Verùm"</note> there must be the word *Gold* <note>Latin: "Aurum" — the translator is suggesting the original text should have read "But Gold..."</note>: so that one must read *But Gold, just like a grain, etc.*, otherwise it would make no sense. And I translated it thus, although it seems there is still something more to be said.

Next, in the same Chapter, page 31 of the Latin: *In the latter way it is called living, because it is thus in potential, which potential within a few days is able to be brought into action; then Gold will no longer be gold, but the chaos of the Sages* <note>original: "Posteriori modo vivum dicitur, quia sic est in potentia, quæ potentia intra paucos dies in actum deduci valet; Aurum tum ampliùs non erit aurum, sed Sophorum cahos."</note>. ...lovers of Science, the *Complaint or Remonstrance of Nature*, the *Alchemist's Answer*, and other pieces in Verse, along with the *Testament of Arnaud de Villeneuve* <term>Arnaud de Villeneuve (c. 1240–1311): A famous physician and alchemist. > *Truly, by a heat more vehement than is proper, this spiritual nature, struck as if by the mallet of death, becomes passive from active, and becomes bodily from spiritual.* <note>original Latin: "Vehementiori verò quam par eſt calore, ſpiritualis hac natura, malleo quaſi mortis percuſſa de activo fit paſſivum, de ſpirituali ſit corporale."</note>

A little later in the same Chapter: *Sometimes like islands, small, sending out spikes etc. in the waves* <note>original Latin: "Interdùm inſulas quaſi, exiguas, ſpicas &c. emittentes in undis"</note>. In Chapter 22, page 60 of the Latin text:
> *It is the slime in which the soul of gold is joined with Mercury, so that they may afterwards produce Adam and his wife Eve.* <note>original Latin: "Eſt limus in quo auri anima cum Mercurio jungitur, ut poſteà Adamum ejuſque Evam uxorem producant."</note>

# REMARKS.

...that I had not translated the word *Magi* <note>original French: "Mages." In alchemy, this usually refers to the "Wise Men" or masters of the hermetic art.</note> in Chapter 3.

# T A B L E.

**To adduce**, to produce, to allege; from the Latin *adducere* <note>meaning to lead or bring toward</note>.
**To affirm** <note>original French: "Affermer," which in modern usage means to lease, but here relates to "affirmations"</note>, affirmations.
**To inflame** & **To enkindle** <note>original: "Afflamber" & "Emflamber"</note>, to incite, to set on fire. It comes from *Flambe* for *Flame*; we still say "to flame" <note>French: "flamber"</note>; from the Latin *flamma*.
**Philosophers' BRASS**, <term>Airain des Philosophes</term>. A Term of the Art; which signifies the same thing as the Philosophers' Gold, which they otherwise call Laton <term>Laton or Latten; a brass-like alloy used symbolically to describe a stage of matter in the Great Work</term>.
**Albification**, whitening or bleaching, the action of making white.
**ALCHEMY**; <term>Alchymie</term>. A word composed of the Arabic Article **Al** and *chemistry*. See the Preface.
**Allegory**, a Greek word <note>original: "allegoria"</note> which signifies that the words must be explained otherwise than in their natural sense; when one says one thing and means another.
**AMALGAM** from which comes *Amalgamation*, is a corrosion of the metal by the mixture of Quicksilver <note>Mercury</note> that is placed with it.
**SOUL**, <term>Ame</term>. The Philosophers call "soul" that which is naturally volatile upon the Fire. See **Body**.
**To bring forth**, <note>original: "Amener"</note> to produce; "reasons brought forth" means produced or alleged; it comes from "to lead" <note>original: "mener"</note>; which comes from the Latin verb *minare* <note>original Latin: "mino," meaning to drive or lead</note>.
**To prepare**, <note>original: "Appareiller"</note> to make ready, **Prepare**, make ready; it comes from "preparation" <note>original: "Appareil"</note>.
**Philosophers' SILVER**, <term>Argent des Philosophes</term>. It is like the proper matrix <note>womb or vessel</note> suited to receive the Seed and the Tincture of the Sun. *Hortulanus <note>a 14th-century alchemist, author of a famous commentary on the Emerald Tablet</note> chapter 4, page 5.* *Philalethes* calls it the "white gold" which is more crude, and which is the feminine seed into which the mature Gold—otherwise called the "red laton"—casts its own, to produce the Philosophers' Hermaphrodite <note>The symbolic end result of the union of male (sulfur/gold) and female (mercury/silver) principles</note>. *Chapter 1, page 239.* In a word, it is the Mercury of the Philosophers.
**QUICKSILVER**, <term>Argent-vif</term>. This is quicksilver or common mercury.

# T A B L E.

**To argue**, to reason, to prove; from the Latin *Arguere* <note>original Latin: "Arguere," meaning to make clear, demonstrate, or prove</note>.
**Arse**, burned; it comes from the Latin *Arsus* <note>original Latin: "Arsus," meaning parched or burned</note>.
**Aries** is one of the twelve signs of the Zodiac, which we call *the Ram or Sheep*. The Sun entering this sign around the 20th of the month of March creates the Spring Equinox. *The Belly or House of Aries* is one of the mysterious terms of the Art <note>The "Art" refers to the practice of Alchemy</note>. Philalethes <note>A famous 17th-century alchemist, likely Eirenaeus Philalethes</note> says in Chapter 2 that the first Philosophers sought and found the active Sulfur hidden in the house of Aries. The Cosmopolite <note>The pseudonym of Michael Sendivogius, a renowned Polish alchemist</note> in his Enigma says that the Steel of the Philosophers is found in the belly of Aries, as was noted in the explanation of the word *Steel*. Fabri <note>Pierre-Jean Fabre, a French physician and alchemist</note> in *the Notes* he wrote on the Treatise on the Oil of Antimony by Roger Bacon, says that Antimony is called Aries because it is attributed to this sign; and that the Water hidden in the belly of Aries is the Water that dissolves gold with a true dissolution; the Mercury of Antimony is, consequently, the true solvent of Gold, because it is the Water hidden in the belly of Aries. This clearly shows that Fabri never knew anything about Philosophy <note>The author uses "Philosophy" here to mean the true understanding of alchemical principles</note>. The Author of the Treatise titled *Rare Experiments on the Mineral Spirit* took it upon himself to explain *The belly of Aries* literally as chamois skin *or sheepskin*, through which one passes Mercury to clean it. This (no offense to him) is certainly not the work of as clever a man as he wishes to appear.
**Athanor**, a word of the Art meaning a tower where one places charcoal to maintain a continuous fire in a furnace joined to it; it comes from the Greek word <term>immortal</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀθάνατος" (athanatos); so named because the "ever-burning" fire never dies out</note>.

**To give** [Bailler], to grant, which is a term heavily used in the Courts of Law <note>original French: "Palais," referring to the Palais de Justice in Paris</note>.
**SEA BATH** [Bain Marin], so named because the Vessel placed inside is bathed there, as if in a Sea. This Vessel is usually a **Cucurbit** or **Gourd** <note>A gourd-shaped laboratory flask</note> made of Glass, Earth, or Copper, in which something is placed for distillation or for digestion: For to circulate <note>A process of continuous distillation where the vapor returns to the base</note>, a different kind of Vessel is needed, or at least one must add a **blind head** to the Cucurbit, that is to say, one that is sealed. The Sea Bath is called *the vicar of the horse’s belly*, or horse manure piled up and heated by itself, where vessels are placed for digestion or to perform circulation. This Bath is prepared in a cauldron or another Vessel, in which the Cucurbit is placed and secured with hay; then the cauldron is filled with water which is heated or boiled as the operation requires, and the water that evaporates is replaced with more hot water. Some call it the **Mary’s Bath** [Bain Marie], intending to say that it was invented by Mary the Prophetess <note>A legendary alchemist, traditionally identified as Miriam, the sister of Moses</note>, whom we believe to be the sister of Moses, and under whose name we have a Treatise on Philosophy. But in all likelihood, the word Mary has been corrupted, like many others, by ignorant Apothecaries, who...

**BODY**. The Philosophers <note>Alchemists often referred to themselves simply as "The Philosophers"</note> call <term>Body</term> [Corps] not only that which has three dimensions—width, length, and depth—but everything that can withstand fire, which they otherwise call <term>Fixed</term> [Fixe]; just as they call <term>Soul</term> [Ame] everything that is naturally volatile upon the fire; and <term>Spirit</term> [Esprit] that which retains the <term>Body</term> and the <term>Soul</term>, and joins and unites them together, so that they can no longer be separated.

## H

**HERMES**, Trismegistus; these are two Greek words which signify Mercury "thrice-great," or "three times very great." See the Preface <note>Hermes Trismegistus is the legendary Hellenistic figure credited with authoring the Hermetic Corpus, the foundational texts of alchemy and Western esotericism.</note>.

**HERMETICALLY**, to seal hermetically, that is to say, to seal with the "seal of the Philosophers." This is done when one heats the neck of a glass vessel, such as a **Matrass** <note>A Matrass is a long-necked glass flask used in distilling and infusions, often called a "bolt-head."</note>, until it is red-hot, and then twists it with pincers or flattens and joins it so perfectly that there is no opening remaining.

**HERMAPHRODITE**, a Greek word composed of *Hermes* <note>original Greek: Ερμης</note>, which signifies Mercury, and *Aphrodite* <note>original Greek: Αφροδιτη</note> which means Venus; as if one said "composed of Mercury and Venus." Mythology says that he was the Son of Mercury and Venus, who possessed the members of both sexes, and was both male and female. This is why we give this name to anything that has both sexes, being male and female all at once <note>In alchemy, the "Hermaphrodite" or "Rebis" represents the successful union of opposing principles, such as spirit and matter or sulfur and mercury.</note>. It is otherwise called **Androgyne**, from the Greek word *Androgynos* <note>original Greek: Ανδρογυνος</note> which signifies man and woman.

**HETEROGENEOUS** or Heterogenea, a Greek word which signifies a thing whose parts are of different natures, such as the parts that compose the body of plants—which are the bark, the wood, the leaves, etc.—and those of animals—the skin, the flesh, the bones, and so on.

**HOMOGENEOUS**, a Greek word which signifies a thing in which all parts are of the same nature and species, just as all parts of Water are water.

**Ligation** <note>original: "Ligature"</note> page 300. To preserve the vessel with its ligation, that is to say, to keep it well-sealed.
**Linear**; from the Latin *lineare* <note>original: "lineare"</note>, that is to say, that which goes straight forward, uniformly and equally, from the beginning until the end: the principal quality of the line being to be everywhere uniform and straight.
**Liquefaction**, the operation by which one reduces a solid thing into a liquid; from the Latin *liquefactio* <note>original: "liquefactio"</note>.
**Moon**, a term of the Art <note>In alchemy, "the Art" refers to the practice of the Great Work.</note>, which signifies **Silver**, and is marked by a Crescent turned from right to left. See **Silver**.

**Lute**, a word of the Art; from the Latin *lutum* <note>original: "lutum," meaning mud or clay</note>, this is the mortar that the Philosophers make to seal and coat, or encrust, their glass vessels, so that they may better resist the fire.

## M

**Magistery**, a term of the Art which signifies the **Great Work** <note>The "Magistery" or "Great Work" (Magnum Opus) is the ultimate goal of alchemy: the creation of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>; from the Latin *Magisterium* <note>original: "Magisterium"</note>. See the Preface. Magistery is also a chemical operation by which a mixed or composite body is so prepared by the chemical Art, without one performing any extraction; so that all its homogeneous parts are preserved and reduced into a more noble degree of substance or quality, through the separation made only of its impurities.

external purities. Béguin <note>Jean Béguin (c. 1550–1620) was a French chemist and author of the *Tyrocinium Chymicum*, one of the first chemistry textbooks.</note>, book 2, chapter 19. Such is the Magistery of Pearls, of Coral, etc., so much so that all preparations of **Metals** are but Magisteries, or the refinement of their Bodies.

**MERCURY**, one of the seven Planets, which is marked with a circle having a Crescent above and a Cross below the circle <note>The astrological and alchemical symbol for Mercury: ☿</note>. It is taken for **Quicksilver**, both the common kind and that of the Philosophers—that is to say, the Mercury that the Philosophers make. For this purpose, Philalethes <note>Eirenaeus Philalethes was a famous 17th-century alchemist, often identified as George Starkey.</note> says in Chapter 1 that it is a Child they form, not by creating it, but by drawing it out from the things where it is enclosed, through the cooperation of Nature and by a marvelous artifice. Thus, it is not found on the earth ready-made and prepared for the Work, as is stated in chapter 13 by the same author. They otherwise call it their **Salt**, their **Moon**, their **White Gold**, the **Female**, their **Pontic Water**, their **very sharp Vinegar**, which has the power to dissolve common Silver and Gold and to resolve them into their own Mercury, which is their seed. The Philosophers say it is **Hermaphrodite** <note>In alchemy, a hermaphrodite represents a substance that combines both "male" (hot/dry) and "female" (cold/moist) principles.</note>, that is to say, male and female, and that it is volatile; this is why they call it the **winged Dragon**. But it becomes fixed <note>To "fix" a substance means to make it stable and resistant to evaporation when heated in fire.</note> by means of the **Sulfur of the Philosophers**, which it brings back to life by dying, and thus becomes their **Salamander** which lives in the fire <note>The salamander was a mythical beast believed to endure fire without being consumed, symbolizing the final, stable state of the alchemical matter.</note>.

**REVERBERATORY** <note>original: "REVERBERE"</note>, Reverberatory fire, which is to say where the flame circulates and returns from above onto the matter, as the flame does in an oven. It is a full reverberation when the fire has no passage through the top; and a half reverberation when the middle of the furnace is open and only the sides are closed, such that the circulation of the fire is only half-complete.

**Rubification**, reddening; the action by which one reddens something, or causes it to become red; from the Latin *rubificatio*.

**TINGING**, a technical term marking one of the perfections of the Philosophers' Elixir, which to be complete must be in powder form, melting, penetrating, and tinging <note>coloring or staining</note> either white or red. **TO TRANSMUTE**, from which comes "transmutation," a term very commonly used in the Art <note>Alchemists frequently referred to their practice simply as "the Art."</note> to signify the change of imperfect metals into Gold by means of the Elixir. This should rather be called the "perfection" of imperfect metals, since they were intended by Nature to reach this perfection, being all composed of the same matter; however, the impurity of their Matrix—that is to say, the place where they are formed—prevents them from achieving it.

*Transverses*, transverse ways, which go across or do not go straight. Trevisan <note>Bernard Trevisan (1406–1490) was a legendary alchemist who allegedly spent his life and fortune seeking the Stone.</note>; from the Latin *transversus* <note>meaning turned across</note>.

**TRITURATION**, as if one were to say grinding; the action by which one grinds and reduces a solid body into small parts through bruising; from the Latin word *triturare* <note>original: "triturare," to thresh or grind grain</note>.

## ROYAL PRIVILEGE.

**LOUIS** <note>This refers to King Louis XIV of France, who reigned from 1643 to 1715.</note> by the Grace of God King of France & of Navarre; To our beloved and faithful Councilors, the Members of our Courts of Parliament, Masters of Requests in ordinary of our Household, Provost of Paris, his Civil Lieutenant, Bailiffs, Seneschals, their Lieutenants, and other our Justices and Officers whom it may concern, Greetings: Our beloved CHARLES ANGOT, Bookseller of our good city of Paris, has represented to us that with great effort and expense he has recovered several curious Treatises on Chemistry <note>original: "Chymie." In this period, "Chymie" encompassed both what we now call chemistry and the spiritual/transmutational practice of alchemy.</note>, composed by the most famous Authors and Philosophers of antiquity and modern times for the transmutation and perfection of Metals; Namely, the Emerald Tablet <note>The "Tabula Smaragdina," a foundational cryptic text of Hermeticism</note>, the Seven Chapters of Hermes with the Commentaries, the Books of Geber, of Morienus, of Khalid, of Mary <note>Mary the Jewess, a legendary female alchemist credited with inventing the *bain-marie* or water bath.</note>, the Assembly of the Philosophers <note>original: "la Tourbe des Philosophes," or *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note>, the books of Artephius, of Synesius, the Chemical Art of Ficino, of Arnaldus de Villa Nova, of Raymond Lully, of Flamel, of Bernard, Count of the Trevisan March, of Bacon, of Ripley, of Haly, of Basil, of Levinus, of Meun, of Zachary, the Great and Small Peasant, the Treatise entitled Philalethes <note>The pseudonym of Eirenaeus Philalethes, an influential 17th-century alchemist.</note> or the Open Entrance to the Closed Palace of the King, the Fountain of the Lovers of Science, the Complaint or Remonstrance of Nature and the Alchemist's Response, the Chrysopoeia <note>The art of making gold; from the Greek *khrusopoiiā*.</note>, and the Golden Fleece of Augurello, and other Treatises in prose and in verse on the same subject; which he has newly caused to be translated and exactly revised by a very expert person, and desires to bring to li- <note>The text cuts off here at the syllable "lu-", likely the beginning of "lumiere," meaning to bring to light or publish.</note>

<summary>This page contains the official royal license granted to the bookseller Charles Angot, listing an extensive collection of famous alchemical works he intended to publish as a single compendium. It serves as a "who's who" of Hermetic and alchemical authorities recognized in the 17th century.</summary>

...first and to have them printed as a single collection <note>original: "en un corps."</note> should he have our necessary Letters for this purpose, given the heavy expenses he has been obliged to incur for the said research. **FOR THESE REASONS**, wishing to treat the Petitioner <note>original: "l’Exposant." The person applying for the legal protection of the privilege, in this case, the bookseller Charles Angot.</note> favorably and to provide him with the means to recover his costs, we have permitted and granted, and by these presents do permit and grant, the right to Print or have Printed the said Treatises on Chemistry <note>original: "Traittez de Chymie." As noted previously, this term included both chemical science and the art of alchemy.</note>, jointly or separately, in one or several Volumes, in such margins, typefaces, and as many times as he sees fit, during the span of nine consecutive years, beginning from the day that each Treatise has finished being Printed: To sell and distribute them throughout our Kingdom. 

We forbid all Booksellers <note>original: "Libraires." In the 17th century, the roles of bookseller and publisher were often combined.</note>, Printers, and others, from Printing, selling, or distributing the said Books under any pretext whatsoever, even if of foreign printing or otherwise, without the consent of the Petitioner or his successors, under penalty of confiscation of the counterfeit copies, fifteen hundred livres <note>The "livre" was the currency of France; fifteen hundred was a very substantial fine, intended to deter literary piracy.</note> in fines, costs, damages, and interests; on the condition of placing two copies in our public Library, one in that of our Castle of the Louvre, and another in that of our very dear and faithful Knight, Chancellor of France, the Lord Séguier <note>Pierre Séguier (1588–1672) was a high-ranking official who controlled the licensing of books in France.</note>, before offering them for sale, under penalty of nullification of these presents. Regarding the contents of which, we command and enjoin you to allow the Petitioner to enjoy them fully and peacefully, ceasing and causing to cease all disturbances and hindrances to the contrary. We desire that by placing an extract of these presents at the beginning or the end of the said Books, they shall be held as duly notified. **WE COMMAND** and order our first Bailiff or Sergeant to perform...

**L**OUIS, by the Grace of God, King of France and Navarre; To our beloved and loyal Counselors, the members of our Courts of Parliament, Masters of Requests in ordinary of our Household, the Provost of Paris, his Civil Lieutenant, Bailiffs, Seneschals, their Lieutenants, and our other Justices and Officers to whom it shall appertain, Greetings: Our beloved CHARLES ANGOT, Bookseller of our good city of Paris, has represented to Us that with great effort and expense he has recovered several curious Treatises on Chemistry <note>original: "Chymie." In the 17th century, the terms chemistry and alchemy were used interchangeably to describe the study of matter and the pursuit of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, composed by the most famous Authors and Philosophers of antiquity and modern times for the transmutation and perfection of Metals; Namely *the Emerald Tablet, the seven Chapters of Hermes with the Commentaries, the Books of Geber, of Morienus, of Khalid, of Mary <note>Mary the Prophetess, an early alchemical figure often associated with the invention of the "bain-marie" or double boiler.</note>, the Assembly of the Philosophers <note>original: "la Tourbe des Philosophes," usually known by its Latin title, Turba Philosophorum.</note>, the books of Artephius, of Synesius, the Chemical Art of Ficino, of Arnald of Villanova, of Raymond Lull, of Flamel <note>Nicolas Flamel, the famous Parisian scrivener legendary for achieving the Great Work.</note>, of Bernard, Count of the March of Trevisan, of Bacon, of Ripley, of Haly, of Basil <note>Basil Valentine, the legendary Benedictine monk and alchemist.</note>, of Levinus, of Meun, of Zachary, the Great and Little Peasant, the Treatise entitled Philalethes or the Open Entrance to the Closed Palace of the King, the Fountain of Lovers of Science, the Complaint or Remonstrance of Nature and the Chemist's Response, the Chrysopoeia, and the Golden Fleece of Augurello*, and other Treatises in prose and in verse on the same subject; which he has had newly translated and exactly reviewed by a very expert person, and desires to bring to li- <note>The text cuts off mid-word ("lumière"), meaning "to bring to light" or publish.</note>
